subsubtopic: VIEW OF LABOUR CONGRESS OF PROPOSED MULTIPARTITE FORUM TO DISCUSS ECONOMIC QUESTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Labour might I put a question to the Prime Minister? Can the Prime Minister advise us whether the Canadian Labour Congress has in fact agreed to return its representatives to the Canada Labour Relations Council and the Economic Council, and whether the CLC has agreed to the labour minister's so-called multipartite national forum?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: VIEW OF LABOUR CONGRESS OF PROPOSED MULTIPARTITE FORUM TO DISCUSS ECONOMIC QUESTIONS
speechtext: On the first point, I am not aware of anything which has been said by the CLC. On the second point, 1 would remind the hon. members that the CLC itself asked for a tripartite set-up. They asked for this some time last summer in several meetings with myself and members of the cabinet. We have agreed to proceed along these lines if we can put a project together. So there is an arrangement in theory between us to have a tripartite, and perhaps eventually multipartite, group meet, but at this stage 1 think it is premature to say that the details have been fixed.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. Considering that we now have the highest number of unemployed in Canadian history, would the minister inform the House why he has permitted officials within his department to operate a quota system, the purpose of which is to disentitle claimants to unemployment insurance benefits to which they ought to be entitled? There should be a white paper which can stand on its merits and be revised in the light of intelligent criticism. Plans which affect the lives of thousands of people and the economic health of communities from coast to coast should not be swathed in secrecy.
I put the position plainly. It is the position which the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce indicated prior to Christmas he would take-that he would shortly make a statement setting out the position with regard to decentralization. Mr. Speaker, the government suffers from a congenital problem. It finds it impossible to do anything in an open and plain manner. I know of no government in modern times which can take a principle, a reasonable principle like decentralization, and so twist it and warp it as to make it unrecognizable.
I asked the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) a question with regard to a specific department. The hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir) also directed a specific question on this subject. What I tried to say in the press release, and what the Globe and Mail correctly reported me as saying, was that we have had enough of the government trying to capitalize on movements. These decisions affect the receiving municipalities. They affect public servants, for example, husbands and wives who may be employed in different departments of government-one of them is suddenly uprooted and moved away. These are important considerations. What the leader of my party, what the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys and others have asked for is disclosure by the government, in the House of Commons, of what it has in mind-I have suggested a white paper-so that we could discuss the matter and put forward suggestions. In this way the public service unions will know what is happening, people entering the public service will know what is happening, and public servants generally will know what is likely to take place.
The reason for issuing my statement was, really, justified anger at answers given to questions 1,138 and 1,139 on the

March 7, 1977
Privilege-Mr. Walter Baker
order paper. These answers, given the most charitable interpretation, must be read as meaning all these decisions are internal and that no consultation will take place, that there will be no white paper and no discussion of this important issue of decentralization. I believe I have made my position clear and I hope the minister will retract his statement, one which is unworthy of him, even in good fun.

The House resumed, from Thursday, March 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Basford (for the Minister of Transport) that Bill C-33, to amend the National Transportation Act and the Department of Transport Act for the purpose of defining the objective of the transportation policy of Canada and authorizing the consequential rearrangement of powers and duties relating to transport, and to amend the Transport Act and the Railway Act in respect of freight rates and other matters, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in this debate on Bill C-33 to amend the National Transportation Act. Coming from Atlantic Canada, I suppose I can say I could get complete unanimity on two questions. First, lack of transportation is the popular reason in Atlantic Canada why economic development has not kept pace with development in other parts of Canada. Second, as a corollary to the many transportation problems we are facing, I suppose I could also get agreement from people on all sides of the political fence with the immortal words of a former minister of transport, namely that our transportation policy in this country is in a mess. So on the subject of transportation 1 think there is consensus.
Solutions to our transportation problems vary, obviously, 'depending on where you sit, who you are, and sometimes what political stripe you wear. But quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, transportation is almost above and beyond politics. Those in Atlantic Canada have been frustrated in their continued attempts to try to come to grips with this question. Transportation should provide the base for a proper and balanced development of Atlantic Canada. Yet in the words of a former minister of transport, one of the reasons this has not taken
National Transportation Act
place is that our whole transportation policy, as I have said, is in a mess.
From that viewpoint, Mr. Speaker, let me turn to Bill C-33. Frankly, I do so with trepidation. I wonder whether it is going to resolve the admitted mess into which this government and its predecessors of the same political stripe have placed transportation. What scares me is the fundamental flip-flop of the government in regard to the National Transportation Act passed by this House in 1967. Bill C-231, as it was known, was debated several years ago when I was a member of the House, and 1 heard Mr. Pickersgill, the then minister of transport, continuously expounding all the worthy, positive principles contained in the legislation, including the fact that there was to be created a Canadian Transportation Commission, of which, ironically or prophetically, he became chairman. Never did a minister of this House have such pride of authorship. For not only did he father, sire, wean and feed Bill C-231 which created the CTC, but he found he had to go to his Valhalla and become its first chairman.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Sounds like legislative incest.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
As my hon. friend for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) says, never has there been such legislative incest, with a minister fathering a bill to which he then becomes the nursemaid when he leaves this green chamber. I do not know what the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has in mind if he survives another election, but one thing I do know is that he does not intend to be successor to the present chairman of the CTC, because Bill C-33 effectively castrates the power, authority and stability of the CTC which is charged with the responsibility of solving our present complex transportation problems and the mess which the former minister of transport admitted.
A quick perusal of Bill C-33 indicates that some of its clauses directly remove power from the CTC and transfer it to the governor in council. According to my count, there are 11 clauses in the bill providing that the governor in council shall make policy, not the CTC. The CTC will be the implementer, as I understand it, of ministerial discretion emanating from the minister's office. As a sequel, Mr. Speaker, there is another interesting provision in the amendments in Bill C-33 which provide that the minister shall, or may, do such and such and so and so. This appears in five separate places. For all practical purposes, the CTC will have no basic power in policy-making.
This will create confusion in the sea of confusion and will pile mess upon mess. Parliament is supposed to be supreme: We are always hearing those words related to interpretations of the Broadcasting Act or to the decisions of the CTC-that the minister cannot do something or other because it is not the will of parliament and he would not want to touch the vague, esoteric, undefinable will of parliament. The minister can claim that he is no longer going to hide behind the will of parliament and that all problems of transportation will come

March 7, 1977
National Transportation Act
to his desk. In the House and in committee he will be exposed to legitimate questions, and it will be incumbent upon him to reply to those questions because he can no longer use the CTC as a decoy. That is the reply to the supposed argument of the minister.
The recent history of transportation in this country bothers me in regard to the minister and his predecessor. If he had been allowed to exercise ministerial discretion, many parts of the country, not just Atlantic Canada, would have been adversely affected. I will explain that point in the next few minutes.
This is an extreme bill, in a vital area that is fundamental to the economic development of the country. It is too important to have the power delegated, in effect, from this chamber to the minister's office and, in effect, to de facto neutralize the CTC. No one in this chamber would complain that when the chips are down there has to be political control. The minister appoints the chairman and the commissioners of the CTC. A lot of them are very good friends of his and some have been good members of this House. That is a different thing from the political science theory, however, that there has to be political control of the decision- and policy-making right in the minister's office without the benefit of public ventilation of those policies which the CTC now provides.
To have the CTC emasculated in the way this bill intends, with the minister responding to the political whims, for political survival, that happen from time to time, will not give us what we need in this country either in transportation or in the economic fabric of the land-and that is continuity and stability in policy-making. Regardless of political stripe, I think a minister of transport can handle the day to day problems, the complex, conflicting and competing claims of transportation and bring continuity and stability at least to the CTC. But there should be a review procedure so that if the CTC takes the wrong road or comes up with the wrong decision, the minister can step in. To completely eliminate that initial public ventilation by the CTC would be a retrograde step and would not enhance the development of a transportation policy.
The turnover of ministers is significant, Mr. Speaker. We can take 1968, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was incarnated, as the demarcation point; when he said things which I am sure he will wish he had never said. There have been five ministers of transport since then, starting with Mr. Hellyer to April, 1969, Mr. Richardson as acting minister until May, 1969, Mr. Jamieson-and I will have a few words to say about him-from May, 1969, to November, 1972, Mr. Marchand from 1972 to 1975, and the present minister who took office in September, 1975. At the moment, in theory and sometimes in practice, he is the fifth minister since 1968.
Let us look at the other side of the coin. There have been two chairmen of the Canadian Transport Commission since 1968, Mr. Pickersgill and the present incumbent, Mr. Benson. So there have been five ministers of transport and two chairmen of the CTC since 1968. This shows that by its very make-up the CTC will, in an apolitical, non-pejorative way bring a little more stability and continuity to policy-making
[Mr. Nowlan.J
than the ever-changing, revolving musical chairs necessitated by cabinet appointments.
The powers the minister will have through order in council-and there are 11-make him not only the transportation czar of Canada, but he could become the economic czar as well through his interpretation of the rates to be charged for competing commodities and his analysis and definition of a review of what "variable costs" mean. While the CTC might review the formula, the bill provides that the minister could dictate where industries and firms should locate and what should be grown. There is no provision for review by parliament or any real review by the Canadian Transport Commission.
I suggest that a brief history of what the minister wanted to do in the last year or so does not lend any great confidence to giving the minister this blank cheque to make transportation policy without any reference whatsoever to parliament. I became a member of this House in 1965, and since then I have seen many bills delegate power to ministers, in some cases with power of review by parliament or an outside board; but I do not think there has ever been a bill that gives so much power to one minister as Bill C-33. I hope this is not a forerunner of the new telecommunications legislation that is supposed to come before the House.
There have been hints that the Minister of Communications (Mrs. Sauve) wants undiluted, unqualified power directed to her so that she can direct the CTC. We will have a situation in this country in which the Minister of Transport, with unfettered powers in transport, economic planning and economic development, will control the economic side of this country, and the Minister of Communications, if there are similar provisions for delegating power by order in council replacing the power of parliament and changing the position of the CRTC, becoming the czar of culture in this land in all the manifest and various forms affecting broadcasting, films, video and cable. Then we will really be moving a long way down the road to an Orwellian society with Big Brother. Quite frankly, the Minister of Transport has many attributes, but one which would not make me too happy is to have him any more like Big Brother, which is one reason I look at Bill C-33 with a great deal of skepticism and reserve. I do not see, at this stage, why he should be allowed this delegated power.
One only has to look at the recent past involving Atlantic Canada, in particular, when the minister, in the general government restraint program, wanted to change a fundamental and basic provision in our legislation to do with "at and east" rates which help the export of flour to offshore markets. If the minister had his way-as, in effect, the amendment under Bill C-33 would let him have his way-the preferred rates for moving flour to offshore export markets would have been eliminated a long time ago.
The Minister of Transport lacks credibility. Assurances were given to the maritime premiers at the time when a change was made in the restraint bill and the section having to

do with "at and east" rates was deleted. At that time the maritime premiers thought it was deleted for good and that the "at and east" rates would stay. We are talking about a relatively few million dollars-about $4 million to $5 million. An assurance was given, direct or implied, that if that section was removed from the restraint bill so as to help the passage of the bill, the "at and east" rates would not be tampered with and the problem would not come up again.
Yet we hear now, since the restraint bill became law, that the minister intends to bring back the legislation to eliminate "at and east" rates in another way. Quite frankly, under Bill C-33, using some of the powers which we would give him under that bill, if he could get it in place in time, he would not have to bring in another bill but under ministerial discretion, and using powers given to him in Bill C-33, he could eliminate "at and east" rates. Thus, he could get rid of what he considers to be a meddlesome and contradictory situation where we in the east receive preferred treatment in the export flour trade and do not fall completely victim to his theoretical user-pay concept in the transport of goods and people.
What faith can anyone in Atlantic Canada have in the user-pay concept when we hear the minister making a press statement about eliminating, with the stroke of a pen, about $1 billion worth of debt on the St. Lawrence Seaway, and at the same time saying he will charge proper tolls? By "proper tolls" he means to charge double the present rate. Already we have had a howl not only from eastern Canada and western Canada but from central Canada as well about what this will do to the economic development of the whole of Canada. Eliminating, with the stroke of a pen, a debt of almost $1 billion, which has accumulated on the St. Lawrence Seaway, is not in accordance with the user-pay concept. Flow the minister can build credibility by suggesting that this debt can be eliminated overnight or with a stroke of his pen or, in effect, through discretionary provisions under Bill C-33 without, on the other hand, guaranteeing a proper toll structure on the St. Lawrence Seaway with input from all those adversely affected, so that we do not start a new debt, is something I find difficult to accept. The two have to go hand in hand.
We in Atlantic Canada reluctantly went along with the financing of the St. Lawrence Seaway because we believed at the time, and we still believe, that it was good for the national development of the country, even though we knew it would have an adverse effect on Atlantic ports. But to have the debt structure of Atlantic ports on the books and not forgiven with a stroke of the pen, as the minister did with the St. Lawrence Seaway debt, is inequitable and in our eyes is not the proper exercise of ministerial discretion. It makes us very reluctant to grant to the minister the power which he seeks under Bill C-33 in its unamended form.
If he can do with the St. Lawrence Seaway what he intends to do now with the powers given to him under Bill C-33, we in the east will be completely shut out unless we are able to get to his left ear and make sure his right ear is blocked so that he hears no one else speaking in his right ear. Whoever gets to the minister's ear gets his attention. We know his nanny has his
National Transportation Act
one ear-and who else can get his attention when his nanny has it? We do not have confidence in the Minister of Transport because of the way he has abused his own principle of user-pay, and we do not have faith in him.
We wonder what he is going to do with regard to fundamental questions affecting not only all of Canada but especially Atlantic Canada. We do not have to talk only about "at and east" rates which are still legislatively suspended above the House and are still on the minister's desk to do what he wants with them. We can consider the recent debate on former Bill C-61, the maritime code, which was supposed to implement the Darling report which was supposed to do many things for many people and, in effect, would make Canadian ships manned by Canadian seamen serve Canadian ports.
We all know the pluses and minuses of this basic argument. But my point is not to debate the plus and minus of Bill C-61 but to use it as an illustration. If Bill C-33 is put in place, there would not be the opportunity, however rare it might be in the House-and in the words of the Prime Minister we are all nobodies anyway-through the work of such diligent members as the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forestall) and other hon. members with a long-standing interest in the maritime code, to spotlight and bring attention to the provisions of Bill C-61.
While statements were made in the House about the assurances given to the maritime premiers, it turned out, as often happens, that they were not worth anything. When we were younger there used to be something called the Boy Scouts, although this is a pejorative term now. Now they are debating whether there should, be "girl scouts" or "person scouts". In my young days we used to play the Kipling game. You would look at ten objects on the table and say what they were and this would be repeated ten times over. By the tenth time there would be ten other things on the table because, due to the vagaries of human nature and the fallibility of tongue, eye and ear, if you repeat a story several times it becomes garbled. In this case you ended up with different items on the table from the ones the first person saw.
I have been in the House and heard the Minister of Transport state that assurances were given and that they were acceptable to the Atlantic premiers with regard to the maritime code, that there would be safeguards so that the Atlantic ports would not be adversely affected. Less than a year ago verbal assurances were given in this House, but there must have been some slip between lip and ear. Some of the statements were perhaps not reassuring to the Atlantic premiers. Over a year ago the then chairman of the council of maritime premiers, Mr. Hatfield, sent a telex to the Minister of Transport with regard to the maritime code saying, among other things:
The governments of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island are most concerned that the maritime code bill, which includes changes to the coasting trade law, is now before the parliament of Canada, while the assurances given by your predecessor, Honourable Jean Marchand to the council of mari-

March 7, 1977
National Transportation Act
time premiers and to the Premier of Newfoundland in September, 1973, have not been fulfilled.
These assurances, which were made public, included-
Then it lists four assurances which were given, but because of changes in ministers, in this case from Mr. Marchand to the present minister, verbal assurances are sometimes confused, even though they are given in good faith. Changes in ministers can lead to confusion. The maritime code was before this parliament and was vigorously debated. It fundamentally affects any coastal member or community and the economic development of those communities. I suggest that if Bill C-33 had been in place we would not have had to worry about debate. We would not have had to worry about the committee, and we might very well have had the minister move in his own arbitrary and unilateral fashion to develop the changes without proper public scrutiny. Assurances could have been given or written into the legislation.
Something very close to my heart is the movement of feed grains from the west into Nova Scotia, particularly the Annapolis Valley. I am all for developing local feed grains, but with the soil conditions and the need we have, and while we have programs to stimulate development of local feed grains, there is still a fundamental need for the movement of feed grains from the west to the east. This has always been considered basic to Atlantic Canada. However, over the last few years its place on the totem pole of security has not been high enough. Farmers have not been able to make plans; they have not been assured of assistance for moving feed grains east. That assurance slowly slipped away. That item is as sacrosanct as perhaps the Crowsnest pass rates, although it was not embodied in legislation; it is just an item in the estimates. Each year the Canadian Livestock Feed Board and the eastern farmers have to wait to see the estimates in order to know the amount of assistance there is to be for the movement of feed grains.
There is quite a debate going on in agricultural circles and before the agricultural research economic council as to the pluses and minuses with respect to the movement of feed grains. In fact, in an agricultural way I do not think there is any question which has as many cross-currents-geographical, political, let alone economic-as the question of feed grains. Some ministers of transport and ministers of agriculture have said that the subsidy should be eliminated and that the local areas which need feed grains should produce them. I am not today arguing the merits of that position. I am trying to point out that by giving a minister arbitrary power, without public ventilation on this question, we might inadvertently effect a program, which has been pretty basic to much of eastern agriculture, eliminated by the stroke of a pen.
There is Parkinson's law and another law stating that it is more difficult to reverse a wrong decision than to influence the decision before it is made. Once there is a ministerial or bureaucratic decision, the proverbial pride of authorship is involved. Natural ego is involved, and it is difficult to change. Obviously, some factors go into decisions and people do not want to be shown to have made wrong decisions. There is a
[Mr. Nowlan.J
danger in giving arbitrary power to a minister when there has not been prior public ventilation. Giving a minister arbitrary power allows him to make decisions which inadvertently could be wrong decisions, but they are very difficult to reverse.
In terms of "at and east rates" respecting the maritime code, Bill C-61-which was debated over the last couple of years-in terms of the movement of eastern feed grains, in terms of the inequity of the St. Lawrence Seaway debt structure, about which nothing has been done, and there has been no intention either expressed or implied to do anything about the debt structure of the ports of Halifax and Saint John, no Atlantic Canadian member can look with equanimity at a bill giving a minister so much power and allowing him to exercise so much ministerial discretion. Another reason we in Atlantic Canada look with a great deal of skepticism at Bill C-33 is the shift in ministers.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Shifty ministers.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Inadvertently, some of them perhaps have been shifty. The hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) has a basic point there. I want to play back for the record something which has irritated me for several years. The last time Atlantic transportation problems were really debated in this House was when the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) was minister of transport. That was in the 1969 period. At that time the legislation under debate was the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act which involved itself with something we thought up to that time was pretty fundamental to Atlantic Canada, the Maritime Freight Rates Act. We in the east thought that was very basic to us. We asked for some protection and as members of confederation we thought we deserved it. The recommendations of a royal commission of the 1920s were incorporated into a form of subsidy assistance to help us get our goods from Atlantic Canada into central Canadian markets.
The Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act varied and qualified, in effect, certain parts of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. The Secretary of State for External Affairs was then the minister of transport, and one of the reasons that bill became law without perhaps more violent objection from Atlantic members was the assurance given by the minister. We are not babes in the woods. We know that assurances given in the House have no real legislative effect-but they are indications of intent. At that time, on June 17, 1969, at page 10226 of Hansard the minister said that the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act was just the beginning of a comprehensive Atlantic transportation policy. He said it was just one bill, that there would be many other bills and that we should not get too worried because the government would move in a comprehensive way on Atlantic transportation problems. I said earlier that that received the approval of all the people of Atlantic Canada, although there were diverse opinions as to what the full solution should be. Among other things, the then minister said as reported at page 10226 of Hansard:
-I may say in a general way that this is only part of the comprehensive transportation policy which is being evolved for the Atlantic region, and these are measures that it was felt, and I believe hon. members will agree, ought to be
March 7, 1977

put into effect as quickly as possible. There will be, of course, considerable additional legislation ... we will be proposing at a subsequent date amendments to existing legislation or perhaps entirely new legislation.
That was said on June 17, 1969. Later in the debate as it was concluding in that memorable June of 1969, on June 19, as reported at page 10383 of Hansard, the minister said:
When I made reference to this bill as being an interim measure, I want to assure the House that I meant that it is only interim in the sense that it represents a portion of a much broader concept that we hope to develop with the help of the very excellent report of the transport committee in the coming months and on which I will be working during the summer recess.
I was a member of the committee. We toured Atlantic Canada for weeks, brought in a unanimous report and made unanimous recommendations. Concurrently, the Atlantic premiers also made unanimous, comprehensive recommendations concerning Atlantic transportation policy. The minister had both reports in his mind when he said that this bill represents a portion of a much broader concept. He went on to say:
There is no suggestion, and I want to make this perfectly clear to the House, that there will be any significant change in any of the measures which either now prevail or which, I hope, will prevail following the passage of this legislation until and unless this more comprehensive program is brought forward and until there has been full-scale consultation with the premiers and the representatives of the Atlantic provinces.
He said all this on June 19. There was a previous statement made on June 17, 1969. To be fair, there have been changes in official committees working on Atlantic transportation. They have made recommendations concerning transportation. But as for the substance of the matter, as for more comprehensive changes under the National Transportation Act, there has been no change. There has been no platform put forward, no plank of a platform or even a nail of a plank, to do with any concrete program for Atlantic transportation.
I gather that my allotted time is almost up, Mr. Speaker. The minister has read the report the transport committee made in 1969 and the recommendations of the premiers. Nevertheless, remembering the assurances made in the past and given in this House, we on my side of the House are not happy with Bill C-33.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-33, a bill to amend the National Transportation Act, is another instalment of legislation concerning our national transport system, a system once envisaged as a national dream. It has become a national nightmare. The NDP does not support it because we fear its long-term implications for a rational and efficient transport system.
What should a national transport policy include? I shall consider that question, consider what has happened in the last few years, consider what the bill proposes to do, why we think it will fail and propose alternative policies. What should be the goals of any national transportation policy? Surely it must encourage, and not obstruct, the free flow of people and goods
National Transportation Act
in Canada. It must not discriminate against regions either on grounds of geographic location or economic health. We should consider our rail, road, air and marine networks as a means for promoting national unity. All our people must be treated equally. No matter in which region of Canada they live or which goods they process and manufacture, they must have access to various modes of transportation. Surely that ought to be the goal if we are at all serious about designing an adequate national transportation system. Second, we must create an instrument which will give us the framework for undertaking economic and regional development in Canada. If these are legitimate goals, as I think they are-and I hope hon. members accept them as reasonable and obtainable-the question arises, how can we best achieve them?
It seems to me that we must follow a certain course if we are to succeed. First, we must devise a national transportation policy which is an instrument of public or government policy and not an instrument solely of private profit. In other words, our national transportation system must be operated as a public utility. Second, we can only reach the goals I have outlined by replacing the present policy of competition between various modes of transportation with a policy of co-ordination and integration. Third, we must abandon the false premises which the Liberal and Conservative parties accept; that is, abandon the idea of commercial viability and users bearing transport costs, for such ideas are inherent in previous legislation and in the present legislation.
What is the situation in Canada? What is the condition of our country's transportation? Looking at our national transportation system, we see it is in a sad state. It is unco-ordinated. Road, rail and air services are not integrated. Interconnections between different modes are often non-existent. Sometimes you must stay overnight in a town before you can switch to another mode of transport. Timing, schedules and services are bad. Also, the movement of goods is not coordinated. A characteristic of our system is-that it discriminates, a discrimination evident in freight rates and the matter of regional development.
When I say this I think of the dilemma facing less developed, poorer regions of the country, such as the Atlantic provinces, northern Quebec and particularly my region, northern Ontario. Our freight rates are discriminatory. Although the government gives grants to encourage development and job creation in the regions, the planning and hard work of our people is frustrated by a national transportation system which charges discriminatory freight rates and works against the development of regional industry and manufacturing in favour of maintaining the status quo in manufacturing in central Canada. The same can be said about raw materials which we obtain basically from the west and the north of Canada.
When we look at our national transportation system, in addition to the two problems I have mentioned we notice a deterioration of service. One has only to look at the standard of efficiency of rail passenger service, or the phase-out by this

March 7, 1977
National Transportation Act
government of some of the coastal ferry system, to see how the general public is being discouraged from using these facilities and suffering because of lack of service. When we look at the situation we cannot help but agree with the former minister of transport when he stated in this House that the transportation system in Canada is in a mess. It is there for everyone to see. The more fundamental point is to examine why we are in this transportation mess today. How did we get into this situation? One does not have to look far for the reason.
In 1967, this House of Commons was debating the National Transportation Act which organized transportation policy on the basis of competition and commercial viability. In other words, the two railway systems in Canada were to compete with one another and railways were to compete with trucking firms and air transport, and vice versa. In 1967 we were told that was the great salvation to ending the transportation problem in Canada: "Let us have competition, and this will create efficiency. The transportation system will thrive and all the regions and people of Canada will benefit".
Surely any person with a knowledge of Canadian history and geography knows that a policy based on those premises is bound to fail. Canada is a country of vast distances and a sparsely scattered population. Because of the great distances between communities and small population in the various towns and cities outside the large metropolitan areas, if you rely solely on the premise of competition and commercial viability those small communities and regions will not get the service. No profit-making corporation in its right mind will build a railway line, put a truck transportation system or airline into areas in which they cannot make a profit. Therefore, you are faced with a dilemma. Either you ignore the bulk of our population which is in scattered areas of Canada or you go around the system of commercial viability and implement subsidies so that service may be maintained for Canadians in these regions. That is what the government has been forced to do.
The logic of geography, history and economics has meant that we must subsidize our transportation systems so that the poorer, less developed and sparsely populated regions can get rail, air and road services in terms of providing people with a chance to move and to bring in and ship out goods. This is what has happened with regard to the maritimes, northern Ontario and the far north. Without the subsidy system we would not have the service. In the debate in 1966 and 1967 the New Democratic Party pointed out that basic fact. They argued that we could not expect the poor and sparsely populated areas of Canada to pay the total cost. User-pay is not feasible in a country such as Canada. Competition does not make economic sense in Canada when so many areas, because of their size, are dependent on a single mode of service.
To base a transportation policy on the premise of user-pay and commercial viability undoes the whole idea of confederation and what this nation is about. We came together as a nation to pool our resources and our wealth and to share our benefits among the regions. The idea was that through the national government all taxpayers shared the cost of common
[Mr. Symes.j
services, whether they be medicare, old age pensions or access to transportation. If we do not work on the premise that all Canadians should be treated fairly and equally in terms of what they, as Canadians, can expect from the services of this country, we end up making second-class citizens out of people who live in the poorer and less developed regions of this country. What is true in terms of creating equality of condition in social services is also true in terms of transportation services. Transportation has to be looked at in terms of service and not only cost. It has to be looked at in terms of a public service that should be available to all Canadians at a reasonable cost. What I am saying is not some new philosophy. It is not a philosophy peculiar to the New Democratic Party. It has been accepted because of common sense and history. It has been accepted by every municipality in this country.
When we look at the kinds of services that are provided to people we see that fire departments are no longer run on the competitive system. In ancient Rome there were two fire departments. If a house were on fire, each brigade would rush over and the bidding would begin to see which one would put out the fire. We accept the principle that all taxpayers, through their municipal governments, should pay taxes in order to receive common service from one fire department. It is a public utility. The same is true of city sidewalks. We do not have a toll gate on every sidewalk based on the principle that the user pays for walking on that sidewalk. If that were the case there would not be enough money to build sidewalks in a neighbourhood. Therefore, we pool our resources through the common tax system and provide sidewalks to be used for all in the city.
The same is true with the bus services in municipal transportation. If that were done with the user-pay concept, those who depend on bus services would never have that kind of service because the cost would be prohibitive. For that reason, municipal governments must subsidize buses to the extent that revenue falls below costs. The bus service is run as a public utility.
What makes me so angry is that the federal government still fails to recognize the obvious about transportation in Canada-that a competitive system distorts transportation goals and discriminates against users in various regions. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is, unfortunately, still wedded to the indefensible concept of commercial viability as the principal component of a national transportation policy. It is this idea which has produced the mess in which we find ourselves in the field of transport today. The thinking behind this legislation still shows that the government is wedded to the concept of commercial viability and user-pay. It is a principle which can never work effectively in this country.
What does the bill say? Competition is still the norm. There are exceptions in the legislation, a few changes, but they do not alter the basic principle. The bill tells us in effect, "Where a transportation system is mature, the user must pay the full cost of the service". We find that the costing date supplied by
March 7, 1977

the railway companies will be used as the basis for establishing freight rates. As one who comes from northern Ontario, I am concerned that this should be the case, because I know it will perpetuate the kind of discrimination in freight rates which has for so long inhibited industrial development in my area.
Further, the legislation gives the Minister of Transport a blank cheque in terms of the orders he may issue to the CTC on policy matters. I am worried about the danger of putting power of this kind into the hands of a minister who is basically unsympathetic to the idea of public service being the norm when considering transportation policy. When 1 hear the minister talk about selling off certain parts of the CNR which were paid for by the taxpayers of Canada and which, after many years, have now become profitable, my fears become even greater. In my opinion, this would be one of the most backward steps imaginable. The proposal is indicative of the private enterprise philosophy held by the minister in relation to public transportation.
I have stated that the government's transportation policy discriminates against various regions of Canada. In northern Ontario, for example, we possess great wealth in the form of raw materials-minerals and forest products. Over the years we have been hewers of wood and drawers of water. We take the minerals from the ground, cut the trees, load them on to boxcars and ore cars and ship them to southern Ontario or the United States where they are processed for manufacture into goods some of which are subsequently sold to us. Of course, as we export our raw materials we export our jobs. Unemployment in northern Ontario is persistently high. Our people must move out of the region, against their will, to look for jobs in the south where the processing of our raw materials takes place. This persistent lack of job opportunities arises to a large extent from a freight rate system which encourages the export of raw materials as opposed to manufactured goods.
If some businessmen or government agency wanted to set up a plan for processing more of our nickel-for example, in the Sudbury region-or associated metals such as copper, they would find that the level of freight rates would make the venture prohibitive: it would cost more to ship processed goods to southern Ontario than it would to ship nickel. For example, in my constituency of Sault Ste. Marie there is a large steel industry. If we wanted to diversify and carry the processing of the steel further, to embark upon its fabrication for the automobile or the appliance industries, freight rates would work against such diversification. As long as we leave the freight rate system as it is, basically at the discretion of the railway companies to manipulate to their own advantage in accordance with the profit motive, we shall not get the industrial development in northern Ontario that we should be getting.
I turn now to another area of national transportation, the St. Lawrence Seaway. I should like to call attention particularly to what is happening in my area of Sault Ste. Marie. We have one Canadian lock at this important juncture of the Great Lakes. It is a small lock. It has not been upgraded and it is only able to handle about 35 per cent of the ships using the
National Transportation Act
system. There are no tolls on either the Canadian or the United States locks at Sault Ste. Marie, but the Canadian lock provides us with our only option in terms of a Canadian entrance to the upper lakes. Yet the government is hearing representations from the Dominion Marine Association to close the lock as a cost-saving measure.
Mr. Speaker, it costs only $1.1 million a year to run the lock. Closing it would end the Canadian option at that important point on the Seaway system; we would be obliged to rely entirely on the United States facilities. In my opinion, this would indeed be a backward step and I do not think the government would agree to taking it. We should be building a second Canadian lock or, at least, upgrading the one we have in order that we could effectively move goods along the system to the advantage of those who live in my area. In this case the government is in a position where it might reduce subsidies and cut back on costs only to the detriment of citizens in our area who regard the Sault lock as an integral part of the St. Lawrence Seaway system. My plea is that these locks not be downgraded but that they maintain 24-hour operation and be expanded so they are able to fulfil their proper function.
I want to discuss another aspect of our national transportation system. I refer to railway passenger services. Here we can see how the bias of the government is against railway passenger services and in favour of air and bus services. The minister is embarking upon a policy of phasing out one of our transcontinental railway services. Most likely the plan will be to maintain the CPR passenger service from Montreal to Winnipeg and then to split the line into the CN and CPR routes to Vancouver. This will mean leaving communities along the CN line in northern Ontario in the lurch. It will mean unemployment for many railway workers along the transcontinental railway system and, indeed, may mean the death of certain railway towns.
The minister argues that subsidized railways are becoming too costly; therefore he should start phasing out some railway passenger services. The point is that subsidies are necessary to provide service to the people and to keep the cost of goods transported by rail to the regions down to a reasonable level. What the minister fails to tell Canadians, when he talks about the high cost of railway passenger service, is that the government is also subsidizing, but to a much higher degree, other modes of transportation.
In 1973, the last year for which I have figures, all other modes of transportation were subsidized, but indirectly so that we do not see headlines like, "Government spends 'X' millions of dollars on railway subsidies". For example, revenues from air transport paid for only 31 per cent of the costs of that system. Revenues from marine transport paid for only 19 per cent of the cost of operating our marine services. As for road transport, revenues paid 64 per cent of total operating costs. However, revenues gained by the railways paid 74 per cent of the cost of operating the railway system. So that the argument of the minister that he is paying too much in the form of

March 7, 1977
National Transportation Act
subsidies to the railways just does not hold water, in light of the evidence.
The federal government is building airports and paying personnel to operate those airports. This is a form of indirect subsidy. We know that federal and provincial governments build roads and a new highway today costs about $1 million per mile. That is a form of subsidy to the truckers and private automobile users. The railways, of course, build their own roadbed. I maintain that all modes of transport in Canada today are subsidized for the benefit of the user: no mode of transportation pays its own way.
The government has deliberately allowed rail passenger service to be downgraded. The Minister of Transport admitted this in the House on January 29, 1976, when he said, as reported at page 10437 of Hansard:
We have operated extensive rail passenger services in Canada. However, they have been allowed to deteriorate so that Canadians no longer have a fair incentive to use them. This was in no way due to any fault on the part of those who operate the trains, but to a combination of management and government policies which could only produce losses and worsening service.
In the same breath, Mr. Speaker, the minister says that Canadians are not using railway passenger service as much as before, and therefore subsidy payments made by the taxpayers are too high, or they are not necessary, and railway passenger service must be reduced. I submit the policy should be the opposite: we should be upgrading our services to encourage use. Railways are more economic in regard to shipping goods and passengers.
In this regard I should like to refer the House to the total amount of subsidies that are paid. The net subsidy for passenger transportation in all modes in 1974 amounted to $909 million. Roads received 62.7 per cent of that total subsidy; air received 22.5 per cent; the railways received 14.8 per cent. In other words, proportionately less subsidy was paid for rail passenger service than for other modes. In terms of energy consumption, railway passenger service is much more economical that any other mode of transportation. Passenger miles per gallon by a DC-9 aircraft averaged out to 34; a B-727 averaged out at 37 passenger miles per gallon; an automobile averaged 63 passenger miles per gallon; a bus 280; whereas a turbo-train averaged 256; and the LRC averaged 303 passenger miles per gallon. So if this government is serious about energy conservation, it should be promoting more passenger rail services. Needless to say, trains cause less pollution than jets, buses or cars. They are also safer, and cheaper for the passenger in terms of energy costs, which are driving up air fares and the cost of operating an automobile.
The government seems to be allowing the CPR gradually to phase out its passenger services, especially in regions like northern Ontario. For example, the CPR wants to end its passenger service between Sault Ste. Marie and Sudbury, yet in light of the evidence that I have put forward it seems to me that logic dictates that the service should be upgraded. We would then be able to co-ordinate schedules and introduce a fast, efficient regional train service in the Sault Ste. Marie-Sudbury-Toronto corridor and the Sault Ste. Marie-Sudbury-Montreal corridor. Upgrading can take place in other areas

too. As the Canadian Railway Labour Association said in its brief to the cabinet:
For example, CN has estimated that 3'/5-hour train service (competitive with the comparable air trip time) from Toronto to Montreal can be accomplished for $150 million in right-of-way upgrading. By comparison, a new cutoff in Montreal connecting route 20 with the northern autoroute to Mirabel will cost approximately $130 million.
So there is much that can be done in terms of relative costs to make the railway service the kind of service it should be and which Canadians expect it to be. The Liberal government has reneged on its past election promises to create viable passenger service between the regions and to grant money to promote a mass transit system in the larger cities. In past policies, in the policy that is implied in this bill and in other announcements, the Minister of Transport is persisting in the commercial viability, competition and user-pay concept. This is a concept which, sad to say, will discriminate against regions and those who must depend upon rail and other services to promote, co-ordinate and integrate an efficient and economic transportation system. It seems to me that this government is going to repeat the mistakes of the past and will not solve the problems of regional development, of fair cost and access to the services that Canadians expect, if it continues with this legislation and the kinds of precepts the minister has announced.
We know we have an enthusiastic and capable work force in the transportation system whether it be rail, air or marine service. They are the backbone of the system and anxious to serve the public, but they want to be treated fairly. This government's actions in terms of lack of safety and job security, as well as in wages and salaries-the Anti-Inflation Board has rolled back the legitimate wage demands of the workers- are undermining the transportation system. Mr. Justice Hall of the Supreme Court, after looking at all the evidence, came to the conclusion that in 1975 railway workers should have received a 13 per cent wage increase. The Anti-Inflation Board arbitrarily rolled that back to 9.3 per cent, undermining the morale of these very competent workers.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I submit that unless we design a system of national transportation to provide reasonable service at reasonable cost and equity for the regions of Canada, we will be doing a disservice to the Canadian people. It is my opinion that this government, and specifically this legislation, is doing that disservice.

speakeroldname: Mr. Art Lee (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to enter this debate. The legislation we are dealing with today is of utmost importance to Canadians. My province of British Columbia entered confederation because of a national transportation policy that resulted in the building of a national railway. Chinese workers were recruited in large numbers to work on the railway that was to bind this nation together. My grandfather was one of those nation-builders. It is because I have an awareness of that history that I applaud the government in its initiative to redefine the framework that would provide us with a transportation policy to meet Canada's future needs.

I welcome the stated policy of the government. Commercial viability, wherever possible, ensures the earnest attempt to minimize government intervention in the marketplace. Equally gratifying is the policy's recognition that some regional areas or some parts of the transportation system where services are required in the national or regional interest but cannot be viably operated on a commercial basis demand the federal government's active support of direct or indirect financial help.
The movement toward re-establishing the policy authority within the government will unquestionably enable the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to take a much more positive role in developing transportation policies. The initiative to strengthen the minimum and maximum provision of the railway freight rates act is welcome news to westerners. 1 urge the government to proceed as quickly as possible in this area so that westerners will not continue having to pay a disproportionate amount of freight for manufactured goods from eastern Canada. Westerners will also welcome the stated provisions to regulate the practice of long-haul and short-haul rates by railway companies.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) who delivered the speech for the Minister of Transport, spent a considerable length of time outlining the government's current transportation program. Indeed, it is a bold and imaginative one; but, like any other major policy designed to bind this nation together, it has to be flexible to meet the needs of the diverse areas and regions of our great nation. With that in mind, it is my intention to discuss how this program is affecting the people of British Columbia.
The matters I wish to discuss are as follows: first, Pacific Western Airlines; second, shipping subsidies for west coast shipping; third, urban transportation assistance. Recently, the Supreme Court of Canada held that Her Majesty the Queen, in right of the province of Alberta, was not a person within the meaning of that term in the National Transportation Act and the air carrier regulations. The result of this decision was that the air transport committee of the Canadian Transport Commission was without jurisdiction to require Her Majesty the Queen, in right of the province of Alberta, to obtain the consent of the commission to the acquisition and control of Pacific Western Airlines Limited or to inquire into the question of whether acquisition of the shares was in the public interest.
I submit that this decision of the Supreme Court of Canada did not, however, declare that the air transport committee has no authority to govern Pacific Western Airlines as an air carrier. Federal aviation law is still applicable. The committee in the past held that it had jurisdiction to question whether the movement of key officials and facilities was a breach of the airline's licence to provide adequate equipment, facilities and services in British Columbia. Furthermore, the committee has rightly maintained its supervisory power over tariffs and safety matters. But in the interlocutory hearings before the committee in July, 1976, there was no hearing into the important issue of whether the transfer of Pacific Western Airlines from British Columbia to Alberta would not be in the public
National Transportation Act
interest. With that in mind, I strongly urge the Minister of Transport to grant the petition of the British Columbia government.
The petition requests the Minister of Transport to direct that the air transport committee conduct an inquiry to determine whether the transfer is in the public interest. If there is any doubt on the part of the federal government whether it has the necessary legislative authority, I urge it immediately to enact legislation giving it the power to ensure that the Queen, in right of the province of Alberta and any other province that may in the future become engaged in aviation, is subject to federal law.
Mr. Speaker, I take this position because, first, I strongly feel that the government of Alberta, through its ownership of the airline, will not adequately account for the availability and supply of air transportation services for the people and goods to, from and within British Columbia.
Second, I feel that the government of Alberta, through its ownership of Pacific Western Airlines, will not act in the best interests of British Columbia because the removal of any of the administrative headquarters and/or maintenance activities will adversely affect all areas of the province by eliminating the indirect and direct employment and income derived from the airline.
Third, I feel the government of Alberta, through its ownership of Pacific Western Airlines and its declared intention to focus all future northern expansion through Edmonton, will not adequately allow for a proper development of potential air routes between the interior of British Columbia and the Yukon.

speechtext:
Indeed, the minister of transportation for the province of Alberta, the Hon. Hugh M. Horner, is on record in his legislature as stating:
Mr. Speaker, those are the reasons we acquired, in a very bold move, Pacific Western Airlines; so that we could look after the people of Alberta in a very real sense, look after the transportation of goods and strengthen our position in northern development, which is one of the exciting things that will happen in this country in the future. It was acquired, Mr. Speaker, not just as an investment, but as a policy mechanism for the government of Alberta to have some input into how the province developed in the direction that development would take. Let there be no misunderstanding by anybody, relative to the reasons and, indeed, the subsequent acquisition.
Fourth, regional airline policy accounts for the regional make-up and diversity of our nation. But, more important, such policy is a part of national aviation policy. This, in turn, is a part of national transportation policy which helps unify this country as a nation. I feel that if the government of Alberta were allowed to retain ownership, a serious precedent would be established which could lead to other provincial take-overs of regional carriers that would result in the balkanization of national aviation and, in turn, national transportation policy.

March 7, 1977
National Transportation Act
Fifth, I feel that there is no social economic justification for the ownership of PWA by the government of Alberta. It should be the principle of any free enterprise government not to enter into public ownership of any business or industry unless it can be clearly established that there is a social need for government ownership and that such business or industry cannot compete effectively in a free market economy without assistance of public ownership. Pacific Western Airlines has a proven track record that shows it does not need direct government intervention of public ownership. It is probably the only air carrier in Canada recently to have made a profit.
Mr. Speaker, the second matter I wish to discuss is that of shipping subsidies for west coast shipping. Clearly, the events of late should be sufficient proof that active federal support and financial assistance is required. If we are to develop the mid and north coast areas of British Columbia pursuant to the federal government's stated policy of regional and northern economic development, transportation in these areas will have to be aided by direct government intervention. The history and track record of private shippers operating in these areas should be proof enough that the principle of commercial viability is inapplicable. My colleagues, the hon. member for Coast Chil-cotin (Mr. Pearsall), the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson), and the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) have during the past year and a half forcefully made this point.
It is, then, gratifying to hear the Minister of Justice, on behalf of the Minister of Transport, stating that if such a case is made, federal financial assistance and support should follow. He said:
Our view is that the role of the government should vary according to the nature of the services and region concerned. Those services which are well developed and mature should be operated on a commercially viable basis within a general policy and regulatory framework provided by the government. Hence, in those cases where there is effective competition, rates and services should be determined largely through the forces of the marketplace. Yet in other regions or in other parts of the transportation system where services are required in the national or regional interest, but cannot achieve commercial viability or the required degree of technological development, the federal government is prepared to provide active support and financial assistance.
Related to this issue of shipping subsidies is the matter of the maintenance of a work force at the port of Prince Rupert. Since the cessation of Northland operations, the work available to the longshoremen at the port of Prince Rupert has not been sufficient. Recently, the British Columbia Maritime Employers Association and the ILWU presented a joint brief about this matter to the Minister of Transport. In view of the fact that the federal government has committed itself finally to establishing the port of Prince Rupert as another major gateway to the Pacific by building the Fairview dock and indicating that the grain facilities will be expanded, I submit that the federal government should protect its interests in ensuring that there is an adequate work force when the port of Prince Rupert finally comes on stream in the near future.
If there is no adequate work force, this new major gateway to the Pacific would soon have the reputation for chronic labour shortages, and certainly this is not what it needs or deserves. Like the port of Vancouver, the port of Prince

Rupert must be considered a major, integral part of the government's initiative of developing and facilitating western access to the Pacific rim countries.
Mr. Speaker, the third and final issue I wish to comment on is the urban transportation assistance program. When the federal government announced its initiative in this area, it clearly made a commitment to help alleviate the problems of urban transit. The announcement was made jointly by the Minister of Transport and the former minister of state for urban affairs, the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson). I quote from their joint press release dated August 27, 1976, as follows:
The federal government recognizes the importance of establishing an urban transportation policy which will conserve energy and improve the urban environment through a shift in urban transportation use from private automobiles to public transit facilities. At the same time the government has a commitment to restrain expenditure increases which would arise from substantial new federal programs.
Unquestionably, the federal government should be concerned with restraint; and as of late it has been doing an excellent job. Of equal importance, the government should be actively supporting concrete means that will enable it to achieve its goal of energy conservation. I submit that the urban transportation assistance program is one of these means. In view of the high costs of gasoline and road building, I submit this government should be actively supporting and financially aiding public transportation systems in large metropolitan areas.
Approximately half the population in British Columbia live in the lower mainland. The bulk of them are commuters. The lower mainland, in comparison to other metropolitan areas of comparable size, is faced with a dearth of transportation alternatives. Montreal and Toronto can look to subway and freeway systems which do not exist in the Vancouver area. This need for a lower mainland transportation policy was recognized and became an integral part of the Liveable Regional Plan. This is a blueprint of proposals to manage the growth of greater Vancouver. It was funded by the federal Department of Urban Affairs and carried out by the Greater Vancouver Regional District which is our form of regional government for the municipalities in the lower mainland.
The Liveable Regional Plan proposes a five-part strategy for managing growth in the region. Briefly, they are: First, achieve residential growth targets in each part of the region; second, promote a balance of jobs to population in each part of the region; third, create regional town centres; fourth, protect and develop regional open space; Fifth, provide a transit-orientated transportation system linking residential areas, regional town centres and major work areas. It is proposal No. 5 that I wish to discuss in greater detail. Fully cognizant of the complexity of the transportation issue and the cost, the GVRD has proposed a three-part strategy to move people and goods efFiciently and as cheaply as possible. Firstly, it proposes growth management. Essentially, what this means is to put more housing where the jobs are in order to limit traffic growth and ensure proper planning that will enable de-emphasis on the automobile in favour of public transportation.
March 7, 1977

Second, the GVRD has recommended a number of ideas to make better use of existing programs. For example "Turn Down Traffic" talks about car pooling and staggered work hours. 1 should add that this program was funded by the Department of Urban Affairs and is now being fully implemented. Third, there is a need for new facilities. I am gratified to see that the GVRD rejects costly stop-gap auto bridges and freeways. It estimates that today under 10 per cent of the daily trips in the region are made on public transit. With the expressed desire to increase this to 25 per cent to 30 per cent over 10 years, active and financial support from not just the provincial but also the federal government is mandatory.
The GVRD has proposed: first, light rapid transit; second, North Shore passenger ferries; third, suburban rail from Vancouver on the CPR mainline along Burrard Inlet to Port Moody and Coquitlam; fourth, fast bus; fifth, articulated routes for streetcars or trolley buses; and sixth, improved local bus routes. I submit that the proposal of the GVRD emphasizes getting the best transportation bargain. It emphasizes minimizing the need for travel by co-ordinating transportation with growth management. As many hon. members of this House have said, this is even more important because the days of abundant and cheap fuel are gone. The federal Department of Energy, Mines and Resources has accurately painted the future of doubling fuel prices and Canada as an energyimporting nation. These are compelling reasons for the federal government to be the leader in causing a turnabout in stressing efficiency and public transit. Lately the government of British Columbia appears to be in a position to respond to the GVRD and the people. Certainly the federal government should be in a position to respond as well.
Related to this matter of urban transportation assistance is a problem which adversely affects the people of my riding and that of my neighbour, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kings-way (Mrs. Holt). The city of Vancouver has designated a number of city streets in our ridings as truck routes. To name a few, they are Powell Street, East Hastings, McGill and Kingsway. Heavy trucks use these streets, and the result has been an environmental problem of noise pollution and constant danger to life, especially to small children. Since the opening of the National Harbours Board container facility, Vanterm, there has been an ever-steady increase in^the amount of truck traffic on these designated truck routes. Unquestionably, I submit, Vanterm has compounded the problem. With respect to a solution, I have suggested the use of the Grandview cut as the major east-west truck route. Support for this has come from the city of Vancouver. The reason I raise this matter is that the urban transportation assistance program could be used as a source of funds for this proposal.
In conclusion, I again want to congratulate the government and the Minister of Transport for the initiative in this legislation. The re-establishment of policy authority in the Minister of Transport is unquestionably the right move.
