subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE REVIEW OF ALL ASPECTS OF PROGRAMS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give serious consideration to a reference to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs to examine and review all aspects of veterans affairs in relation to (a) the services program (b) war veterans allowances (c) the Civilian War Allowances Act (d) supplementary financial assistance on the basis of need (e) hospitalization and medicare assistance, with particular attention to the results of the progress in the transfer of veterans hospitals to other levels of government or agencies (0 educational assistance for veterans and the pensioned children of the deceased veterans (g) specialized services for blind, deaf, paraplegic veterans (h) counselling service (i) reviewing the need for increasing grants and contributions to the army benevolent fund, the Royal Canadian Legion, Canadian Veterans Association of the U.K., Commonwealth Graves Commission, United Nations Memorial Cemetery in Korea (j) the consideration of grants to other veterans' organizations in Canada (k) examining the need fof improvements under the Pensions
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
Act, with particular reference to the recommendation of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs to provide pensions for widows whose deceased husbands were receiving 48 per cent or less (I) the Pension Commission (m) the Pensions Review Board (n) the Bureau of Pensions Advocate (o) assessing the progress under the special housing program for veterans (p) considering the need for increases in funding towards the Last Post fund and assistance for funerals, burials and headstones (q) reviewing the P.W. Compensation Act and considering amendments to include First World War veterans, escapees and evaders (r) other matters, pertinent to Canada's obligation to its veterans.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is fortunate that our rules provide an opportunity during private members' hour to focus attention on matters which, unfortunately, do not seem to achieve national attention even though the veterans community consists of approximately two million of our population, comprising some 885,000 veterans plus their dependants. They deserve a hearing. Some hon. members are concerned about the veterans of this country. But there are some hard facts to be known, and I think it is time to put them in their proper perspective.
Even though we who hold a particular interest for veterans keep repeating to ourselves that we have the best veterans' legislation in the world, I suggest, that we do not have it. If we did have it we would not be in the embarrassing position, in 1977, some 58 years after World War I, 31 years after World War II and 20 years after the Korean conflict, of not having provided for a veterans' charter which serves the veteran and his dependants, and we should not face the many glaring inequities still existing in our veterans' legislation.
I want to put some further glaring examples on record. Hon. members will not be surprised when I point out, again, the discrimination existing under the Pension Act whereby widows of veterans who died with a disability pension of less than 48 per cent are discarded by the department and thrown into the hands of provincial welfare systems unless the death was attributable to the pensionable condition. Of the 85,724 married pensioners, 68,526 are between the 5 per cent and 45 per cent category, and while many of them may have other income which might preclude the need, there must be a sizeable proportion of widows who are forsaken by the government and must rely on the welfare program. This is an embarrassment to us all.
The inclusion of these widows for pension was a recommendation of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs arising out of the Hermann report on the need to compensate prisoners of war. Naturally, this government turned it down with the excuse that they could not afford to pay the $40 million or $50 million it would cost. I will try to point out the weaknesses still existing in the legislation and explain the discrepancies existing in that the department cannot seem to recognize the lack of equality as between two pieces of legislation.
Under the Pension Act a married veteran receiving a 48 per cent disability pension, with no children, receives $347.88. On his death, his wife receives $417.47, or some $70 more, which is fair and equitable. But the widow of a veteran who was receiving 47 per cent, or just $34.78 less, receives nothing unless-and I repeat-the death was attributable to his pensionable condition.
March 7, 1977

On the other hand, let us look at the war veteran's allowance recipient. If married, he receives $392.49 minimum, or $462.49 on a needs basis. If he or his wife can work, he is entitled to casual earnings of $188 per month, for a total of $580.49. On his death, the widow of the war veteran's allowance recipient is entitled to draw the married rate for one year. She then reverts to the single rate of either $270.16, or $355.16, if she can earn under the casual earnings provision.
I think, too, that we ought to look into the discrepancies which arise form relating disability pensions to war veterans' allowances. These confirm the need for a comprehensive review of the entire question. Let us consider the benefits to be derived under both sides of the veterans' charter. I hope hon. members are paying attention and will recognize the existence of obvious discrepancies. I ask hon. members to consider the following examples and compare benefits, taking into account that one of the benefits is for disability while the allowances are designed for a pre-aging condition.
A single recipient under WVA receives an entitlement of $230.16 which is indexed quarterly. On the basis of need he may be eligible for a further $40 per month, for a total of $270.16. The single disability pensioner, on the same basis, must have a disability of 60 per cent to be eligible for that amount. I think hon. members agree that a 60 per cent disability is pretty serious. Further, if the WVA recipient can work, he can earn $125 per month, to give him a maximum of $355.16. In order to reach that pension level the disability pensioner must have a 60 per cent disability.
I come now to the case of a married war veteran's allowance recipient with no children. His basic allowance is $392.49, and in the case of need he can be eligible for a further $70, for a total of $462.49. The disability pensioner must have a disability of at least 70 per cent to qualify for that amount. If the married WVA recipient can earn a partial living, he is eligible for casual earnings of $188 per month, giving him the maximum earnings of $580.49. This compares with the allowance of a pensioner with an 85 per cent disability.
To take the matter one step further, a married veteran with two children under WVA can reach a maximum earnings figure of $701.27, made up of the basic $392.49 plus $120.78 for two children up to the age of 25 if they are in university or other institution of learning, and $188 in casual earnings. To be entitled to the same amount a disability pensioner must have a disability of 85 per cent.
In addition, there is another variation with regard to drug care. The war veteran's allowance recipient has access to all the drugs he requires, yet the disability pensioner can only qualify for the drugs relating to his pensionable condition. It should be obvious that these discrepancies justify the presentation of my motion, and I ask for unanimous consent to refer the whole veterans' charter to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs.
On the other hand, any veteran who qualifies for a disability pension of 5 per cent, which would give him the meagre pension of $27.82, single, or $34.78 married, is eligible to apply for war veteran's allowance. It should be obvious that
Veterans Affairs
disability pensioners who earn no other income could qualify for a war veteran's allowance far above their present pension. Some of our veterans are not aware of this situation; consequently, they are losing many dollars of income for which they could qualify, and they could perhaps protect their wives after their death since widows of recipients of war veteran's allowance are eligible for allowances.
Statistics show that some 68,524 veterans between the 5 per cent and 45 per cent categories may be losing many dollars of income, to say nothing of the loss of protection for their wives who cared for them through their suffering, or for the widows of veterans. But these inequities are not recognized by the "secret societies" of the government, the experts on veterans affairs. I am referring, for example, to the group known as the management by objectives committee, the organizational effectiveness group and the management advisory services group. It is the job of such organizations to redefine, to keep a watch on legislation affecting veterans and make sure that it is to the benefit of our veterans.
While we are talking about discrimination against widows, I am wondering about the concerns of the status of women council. What are they doing? Clearly, they are not aware of this discrepancy, which only emphasizes the fact of, diminishing concern for the veterans of our country and their widows. I am thinking of veterans or widows with meagre pensions, with pensions based on 48 per cent of disability.
Another matter that indicates that changing conditions require constant attention is the basic rate of pension. In 1972 the rate was finally established relative to the average wage of five public service groups. It has now become obvious, because of an increase in the wages of the people in the public service, that the veteran has fallen considerably behind and that amending legislation is necessary to correct this variance. This question was brought to the attention of the minister forcibly when the Hong Kong veterans wrote pointing out the salary levels of the five categories of public servants on which the 1972 rates were based. They gave the list of the composite group of public service employees. The average earnings were $8,501. Applying the 1976 income tax exemption for a single person, the taxable income was $6,161.
Federal and Ontario income tax on this amount, based on 1976 rates, will be $1,285, leaving a net income of $7,216. They point out, further, that the 1977 annual basic pension rate for a 100 per cent single pensioner is $6,679. Therefore, the pensioner is now behind his counterpart by $536.56 or $44.72 a month.
Another matter which indicates that changing conditions require attention is the basic rate of pension. That change is with regard to indexing of WVA benefits for those over 65 years of age. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and I have brought this utter confusion to the attention of the House. When the veteran is over 65 years of age and his pension is indexed and at the same time his WVA
80010-29'/2

March 7, 1977
Veterans Affairs
is indexed, he loses the war veterans' allowance indexing in favour of the old age security.
Disability pensioners are also losing out on income as a result of the 5 per cent graduation in classes of pension. For example, under one classification pensioners assessed at 18 per cent to 22 per cent are all paid at the 20 per cent rate. Therefore, pensioners at 18 per cent get the same amount as their comrades at 22 per cent. The same situation exists in the other classes. This indicates an inequality which should be reviewed.
While legislation has been introduced to allow shortening of time of qualification of emigrants from five to three years, as pointed out by my colleague from Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), under the new old age security rules, a former resident who had 20 years prior legal service after age 18 would be entitled to receive a full pension abroad without returning to Canada. Even though it does not apply in some cases, is there any reason why a war veteran who has to come back to Canada for 365 days to qualify should not be given the same preference? Changes should be made to assist the World War I veteran.
There is another item of discrimination. Male veterans must be 60 years of age in order to qualify for war veterans allowance while female veterans can qualify at age 55. This, too, should be reviewed and taken into consideration by the committee in order to bring our veterans' charter in line with changing conditions and to recognize the service.
While we who sat on the veterans affairs committee can stick out our chests and boast about the fact that we were able to get compensation for veterans who were prisoners or war, there are many factors that have come to our attention since and which were not included in the act. We either forgot or ignored World War I veterans who were prisoners of war. Even though representation was made, we did not take into consideration the escapee or invader, some of whom suffered more than those who were captured. We failed to recognize the veteran who was incarcerated for only three months. A person must have been incarcerated for at least three months before he can qualify. We failed to recognize that disability pensioners at 90 per cent, who qualified under the prisoners of war compensation act for the largest amount or 20 per cent, loses out by 10 per cent because of the maximum 100 per cent section in the act.
Another main concern of veterans across the country is as a result of the government's decision in 1963 to transfer hospitals to non-departmental agencies. While the principle may have been logical, the results on a good number of occasions leave much to be desired. I can substantiate this statement since I visited, with members of the caucus committee on veterans affairs, some of the hospitals already transferred. Whoever decided on this policy-and I do not quarrel with the decision made in 1963-and promised priority care and that domiciliary care and chronic case beds would be available on a priority basis, as well as active care, was less than capable in projecting the needs of veterans as they grow older and require extended care, more so in 1977 than ever before.

This is borne out by the fact that in the hospitals transferred, waiting time for veterans is up to two years for a bed. A prime example of this lack of attention is the transfer of the Veterans Pavilion in Victoria to the Jubilee Hospital. As a result of the protests by concerned veterans associations in Victoria, several visits were made by the minister and his staff to hear the complaints of those who care. I need do no more than give a comment on a report by the department as to the availability of domiciliary and chronic care beds made just three months ago on November 10, 1976, referring to waiting lists. In Saint John, New Brunswick, there is apparently a great shortage of beds. It is impossible to estimate the waiting time. In Vancouver and Victoria applicants are on a points system, as well as having to wait for a vacancy. The applicant with the lowest points could in some cases wait forever. Is this the way to look after our veterans?
Apart from neglect of Canada's commitment to veterans, the government gave as the reasons for the transfers the fact that they could not keep doctors because active care is not required. This I quarrel with because according to people I have talked to there are enough retired dedicated medical doctors who will care for their comrades. In spite of this, the government is handing over to the provinces not only hundreds of millions of dollars in buildings and equipment but hundreds of acres of valuable land. In addition, they are paying out more millions of dollars to the provinces to provide the care and the beds. Surely, the least a veteran can expect is fulfilment of the commitment made to him by those who asked him many years ago to serve his country. I repeat that these facts emphasize the need for a complete review by the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs before any further transfers of hospital beds are made. In fact, this should be done immediately.
I now wish to deal with the housing legislation. With the approach of the March 31, 1977, deadline for additional loans under the Veterans Land Act, I think it is worth while pointing out that we can now say, "We told them so." I was happy to read in the annual report of the Department of Veterans Affairs that as a result of the opposition forcing the government to extend the act for one year, approval of 1,291 new small holding establishments and 13 new farm establishments was made. Additional loans were made to 1,905 veterans already settled under the act, and a total of 533 veterans were able to build new homes, for a total expenditure of $34 million.
Not only can we say, "We told them so", but we were able to prove the supposed experts wrong, those supposed experts who wrote columns trying to convince the citizenry that they were right, when they did not know what they were talking about. In this connection, I commend Canadian Press for having told our story impartially when we fought and won the battle for some 3,742 veterans, but I am also happy to condemn the few to whom I referred beforehand.

The government was also forced to introduce a new housing program which could be improved by a review by the committee. In this regard I refer to the need to expand the present program to include home repairs, similar to the residential rehabilitation assistance program now in existence, whereby grants of $3,750 can be directed to those on low and fixed incomes of $6,000 or less. In spite of the fact that I keep getting the answer that these grants are applicable to all Canadians, the loans are restricted to areas designated by the provinces, which leaves many veterans out and denies them the opportunity to take advantage of the program, which, again, shows lack of interest in the needs of veterans.
The utter absurdity of the phasing out of the act is borne out by the fact that it was not costing the taxpayer money. It is another example of the failure of Canada's commitment to the veterans, along with the further step by the government to phase out the department. Repayment of principal amounted to $48.5 million dollars, with interest received of some $28 million. I will always hold glory in the fact that our motion, which extended the act, served 3,742 veterans who otherwise would have been left out.
While time does not permit me to cover the remainder of the 17 points in my motion, may I group many of them by pointing out that the government should take a hard look, as a result of inflation, at increasing funding for funerals, burials and headstones under The Last Post fund and other benevolent funds. It is obvious, when one reads the financial statements of the benevolent fund that while the veteran population is decreasing, expenditures are increasing; due, of course, to inflation. When one examines the estimates for this year, it is evident that grants and contributions to the army benevolent fund, the Royal Canadian Legion, the Canadian Veterans Association of the U.K., and the Commonwealth Graves Commission, should be increased. Recognition should also be considered for veterans organizations which are serving the veteran population; I mention in particular War Amputations of Canada which for many years has led efforts to provide improved prosthetic devices for veteran amputees.
1 thank hon. members for extending the time available to me. I could go on for many more minutes. I only hope I have made some impression on the members on the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs and others. I understand there are some 50 veterans still sitting in this House, and they should be proud that the legislation is to be reviewed at the earliest opportunity.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE REVIEW OF ALL ASPECTS OF PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on the motion which has been proposed. It is broad enough in its terms to enable us to discuss a number of subjects, and this afternoon I wish to mention two or three which are of particular interest to me. The first concerns administration of the hospitals which remain the responsibility
Veterans Affairs
of the Department of Veterans Affairs, in particular, the Ste. Anne de Bellevue Veterans Hospital in my riding. The present situation is causing anxiety among both the veterans who work at this hospital and the veterans who are patients there. Their concern arises at the prospect of impending transfer of responsibility to the provincial government in connection with which discussions have been going on for some time.
I have placed many questions on the order paper on this subject and have received a variety of answers. It seems that another hospital presently in the hands of the department in the province of Quebec, the Queen Mary Veterans Hospital, was being turned over to the provincial authority. In fact, a recent answer says there is an agreement in principle that the Queen Mary Hospital in Montreal will be transferred, though negotiations in connection with the transfer have not yet been completed. Since then there has, of course, been a change in the provincial government and it now seems as if this particular transfer is not to take place, at least in the foreseeable future.
The problem in connection with the Ste. Anne hospital is the continuing uncertainty. Employees are worried about their security. They are concerned about their benefits. Moreover, the situation with regard to the patients themselves is not clear. Not all the patients are the responsibility of the federal government. According to an answer to a question of mine on the order paper, there are 845 patients of whom approximately one-third are considered to be a federal responsibility. The other two-thirds, although they may be veterans, are concerned about what might happen to them if the hospital is transferred.
At Senneville Lodge, which is part of the Ste. Anne de Bellevue Hospital, there are 136 patients at the present time. The lodge is a very old building. It was the intention of the federal government to construct a new building, and some $6 million has been allocated for that purpose. It was assumed that if the Ste. Anne veterans' hospital was transferred to the province, along with it might go a lump sum to cover the construction of the new facilities. Nevertheless, because of the delay and the lack of decision nothing has happened and no construction is planned. In fact, at the present time the situation is completely dormant. I therefore propose, and will continue to suggest, that the Department of Veterans Affairs make up its mind by stating there will be no further discussion on the subject for a period of not less than three years or, better still, five years, during which time normal responsibility would be exercised. This would put an end to the immediate anxiety of patients and employees.
In the department itself, the question of morale among the staff is one which must be considered. The recent announcement that many of the branches of the department would be transferred en bloc to Prince Edward Island met with anything but a favourable reaction among employees. A release issued by employees of the department gives expression to this concern and draws attention to the disruption of family life, the main reason given by the overwhelming majority of departmental employees for rejecting the transfer to Charlottetown.

March 7, 1977
Veterans Affairs
According to answers given by employees of the department responding to a Public Service Alliance circular, many members of the veterans affairs component last November rejected the idea of a transfer by some 90 per cent; only 5 per cent favoured the move, and the remainder claimed they were undecided at that time because of lack of information as to the government's intentions. This is understandable. Apparently, according to an announcement by the department, relocation will not take place until 1980 or early 1981, and employees will not be required to consider their decision to relocate until at least another three years. Therefore we have a situation where the employees will not be spoken to until the end of the current year, and they are going to be discussing something which will not happen for at least another three years.
Although I fully support the principle of decentralization, I find it strange that the department should proceed in this manner, leaving everyone so uneasy. Surely if we are going to decentralize the department, the first thing to do is to discuss it with the employees in order to find out precisely what the effect is going to be, to familiarize them with the intentions of the department concerning the problems everyone will have, and then, after all these decisions have been made on location, the cost of relocation and so on, make the announcement. This seems to me to be the logical way to proceed. It is difficult for me to understand why there has to be such a complicated procedure as to talk about three years hence, thus leaving everyone so uneasy.
I placed four questions on this subject on the order paper on October 29 last, questions Nos. 859, 862, 863 and 865, and they are still there today. 1 find it strange that the department is unable to answer the first of these, for example, which inquires how many square feet of office space is presently occupied by these various departments which are intending to move. 1 then asked whether any of the space is rented and, if so, what were the terms of the lease and the termination date. 1 would have assumed that a simple question, asking the Department of Veterans Affairs how much space it was using, whether it leased the space and what were the terms of the lease, covers information that could have been obtained within a matter of a few days at most, and the question answered probably within two or three weeks. However, 1 reiterate that on October 29 the question was put on the order paper and, some five months later, it is still on the order paper. No wonder there is some dismay on the part of the employees.
If I can go back to the release to the employees of the Veterans Affairs Department, it even reiterates that only about half of my questions have been answered, and that most of the responses provided by the Veterans Affairs Department have been uninformative. These questions are put on the order paper for a multitude of reasons, one of which is that information will be made public. In this case the employees themselves would have had a better idea of precisely what is involved in the move. Obviously many of these employees are now well established in Ottawa. Many have purchased houses and have mortgage obligations and so on. Many have wives working in

Ottawa. They have children going to school in Ottawa. Many employees in the department are French speaking employees. Their children go to French language schools. They are asking what is going to happen to them when they go to Charlottetown. Are there going to be school facilities in the French language in Charlottetown? These are normal questions that one would think would be answered prior to announcing any move.
Again quoting the press release in the employees' newspaper:
Mr. MacDonald admitted, however, his department has not analyzed the implications of relocation on DVA staff and no employee assistance policy has been adopted.
I think that is a dreadful admission, and I am sorely disappointed that it has been made by a minister of our own government.
When we are discussing language, some interesting things come from questions. In the whole of the DVA in 1975 there were 122 employees whose mother tongue was English. In 1976 the number had increased to 211, or an additional 89 employees. French bilinguals increased from 732 in 1975 to 786 in 1976, or 54 additional employees. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, this information was given in answer to two questions of mine, Nos. 856 and 1,460 in this session of parliament.
This information raises some interesting questions concerning the attitude of the department toward blingualism. In the national capital region, 39 whose mother tongue is English were bilingual; in 1976 that number had increased to 87, a plus of 48, while those of French mother tongue diminished from 180 in 1975 to 165 in 1976. Note that unilingual employees, French and English, have dropped by 70; and bilingual employees have increased by 34, leaving a reduction in staff of 36 employees. Yet the total of employees in 1975 compared with 1976 shows a decrease of only six employees. In other words, I am even questioning here the arithmetic of the department.
Worthy of note is the fact that the number of bilingual employees has increased from 39 in 1975 to 87 in 1976. This does not mean that they are bilingual in the true sense of the word but probably that they meet the requirements of the department. There are examples where employees have spent a number of months at language school and since they have been in the department have not spoken a word of French. This, of course, is one of the problems all departments are facing these days. In a question answered only last week I suggested that the government should look at the effect on second generation children in a family when there has been an encouragement to bilingualism, we find the situation where the Francophone bilingual tends to become more Anglophone, and the probability is that his children will tend to be more English than French.
In other words, whereas the teaching of French to an Anglophone-in my opinion, sometimes a rather futile exercise in the public service though certainly a very expensive exercise-will not in any way destroy the capability of that family to speak their mother tongue, English, the chances are that the
March 7, 1977

teaching of English in a Francophone family will encourage its descendants to speak the other language, the language most often used in this capital of Ottawa, namely, English.
What we have to face is the fact that the more often used bilingual in the public service, who frankly is the Francophone, is being torn away from his culture by this encouragement toward bilingualism; and I have suggested that the easiest way to handle this is to hire more Francophones at different levels in the public service.
I have brought out these points, Mr. Speaker, because even the Royal Canadian Legion reacted to this announcement of the DVA move. Their concern was efficiency. They support the principle of decentralization, as we all do, but they felt, as I feel, that there have been too many indications that this department has a kind of knee jerk reaction-there is lack of planning, there is no evidence that the move has been planned in advance, there is no evidence that the effects of the lengthy, drawn out discussions concerning transfer of hospitals in the province of Quebec have been adequately considered. The result is low morale among the employees, a situation which, in my opinion, should be corrected by a full investigation.
The motion proposed by the hon. member is complex and not one which in its entirety I would be willing to support. But the principle of looking into the Department of Veterans Affairs I support 100 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend most warmly the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St.Barbe (Mr. Marshall) for having put down the motion that we are discussing this afternoon. He indicated it contains some 17 points, so even he was not able to deal with all of them. I wish to speak about three or four subjects mentioned in the motion, on all of which the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe touched. Before I do so may I say that I welcome the intervention of the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert). In particular I am glad that he raised the question of the proposal to move the Department of Veterans Affairs from Ottawa to Prince Edward Island. I think many of us share his view that we favour the principle of decentralization of government departments but we insist that each case should be looked at on its merits.
The Department of Veterans Affairs exists for the purpose of providing service to our veterans. Some of us are not sure that that angle has been completely looked into in planning for this move. In view of the fact that nothing is going to happen for two, three or four years, I hope the considerations raised today by the hon. member for Vaudreuil will be looked at by the department and the government. I join with the hon. member in expressing regret that there was so little consultation-indeed practically none-in advance of the announcement either with the employees of the department or with the
Veterans Affairs
various units that make up the Department of Veterans Affairs. I could stay on that subject, but I would rather underline a few other points mentioned in the motion which were discussed by the hon. member who put this motion before us this afternoon.
At the top of the list I mention the need to do something about what we all know as the 48 per cent rule. In my view, for the law to continue to deny to the widows of veterans, where a veteran's pension was less than 48 per cent, a pension as of right, is most unfair. The view that there should be pro rata pensions for those widows has been put forward officially four, five or six times to my knowledge. It was in the report of the Woods Commission a number of years ago, and again in the report of the commission headed by Dr. Hermann on the question of prisoners of war. To my knowledge the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs two, three or four times recommended the implementation of Mr. Justice Mervyn Woods' recommendation or the recommendation made by Dr. Hermann. The idea is not just one that some of us in opposition put forward. It has been around for a long time. I think it is fair to say that the evidence will bear out when we discussed this matter in the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs that the officials were ready to comment on it; so it is obvious they have thought about it as well. I plead that it not be allowed to drag on much longer.
Another issue mentioned by the hon. member who proposed this motion is compensation for prisoners of war. We did well a few years ago when we provided compensation for Hong Kong prisoners of war, and again a year or so ago when we improved that compensation and established pensions for those who were prisoners of war in Europe.
One might raise some question about whether the amounts are adequate, but the main deficiencies are those already mentioned by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe. The first is the failure to include prisoners of war from World War I, and I hope we get around to that before they are all dead. There cannot be many left. To try to explain to them that somehow there was a difference, just does not wash.
Then there is the problem of the escapees and evaders. This was covered in the report the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs made to the House after studying the Hermann report. I regret that when the government brought in the legislation these items were left out. They were not forgotten; it was a case of deliberately leaving them out. Like the sponsor of this motion, I think this matter should be dealt with without further delay.
I underscore very heavily the plea made by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe about the rate of the 100 per cent disability pension. It took 40 or 50 years of activity in parliament to get that rate back to what it was when it was first established in the 1920's, namely, a rate that bore some relationship to income in the Public Service of Canada. In 1972 we established that the rate of the 100 per cent war disability pension was to be the equal of the average income of five selected categories in the public service. They are low categories in terms of wages, but at any rate five were selected

March 7, 1977
Veterans Affairs
and their average, taking income tax into account, was established as the basis of the 100 per cent disability pension in 1972.
That decision was made on the basis of a report from a very important tripartite committee which consisted of representatives of veterans' organizations for one part, the Department of Veterans Affairs for another, and the Canadian Pension Commission for the third. When that tripartite committee recommended that the 100 per cent disability pension be established at the rate 1 have indicated, the composite average, it also recommended it continue to be tied to that average. We supported that, and recommended that as the wages of those five groups in the public service went up, the 100 per cent disability should go up by the same amount. I was elated when we got that recommendation from the tripartite committee, and I was elated when the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs supported it.
I can think of another instance-although 1 do not want to tread on any toes in these few minutes-where we have used the composite industrial index instead of the cost of living index, but in this case the government did not accept either the recommendation of the tripartite committee or of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. Instead of saying that the 100 per cent rate would remain whatever the level was for that composite group, it said we would start with an absolute sum for 1972 and after that escalate only by the rise in the cost of living index or the consumer price index. The hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe has already put the figures on the record, but the fact of the matter is that in 1977 the 100 per cent rate, which was the equivalent of the composite rate in 1972, is $536.56 per year, or $44.72 per month behind the composite rate of those five groups in the public service. This is a disgrace, Mr. Speaker. It took nearly 50 years to get back to the original decision of the 1920's. Some of us were afraid that, because of attaching it to the CPI rather than the composite index of those five groups, this would happen. It has happened sooner, however, and gone further than we feared. I suggest that needs to be corrected. But since this is private members' hour, and one of the sins opposition members do not indulge in is to talk till six o'clock. I must wind these remarks to a close.
I want to support the idea that a particular area for overhaul is the War Veterans Allowance Act. I could go into this in some detail, but 1 think I shall make my point by citing a case that is in my mind at the moment because of a letter I received a few days ago. It will demonstrate how unfair this situation can become. I received this letter last week from a woman in the province of New Brunswick, the wife of a veteran who had served six years in World War II. At the end of the war he was invalided home, and he has been in poor health ever since, indeed for more than 30 years. He has been in and out of hospital and he has had all kinds of treatment, but even so the maximum disability pension he has been able to get is only 15 per cent. That being the case, he was entitled to the war veterans allowance, so he got it. When he was 65,

he became entitled to old age security and the guaranteed income supplement. These amounts plus his 15 per cent disability pension have reduced the amount he receives as a war veterans allowance, so that his total is not above the ceiling that is allowed under the War Veterans Allowance Act for a married veteran.
Fine, so far so good. But the wife writes to me and says that she will be 60 in a few weeks and she has been told that she will then have to apply for the spouse's allowance. That is true. The law does not say she must apply, but the law says that if she does not apply for the spouse's allowance she will be treated as if she is getting it and the war veterans allowance will be cut off. She will be treated by the War Veterans Allowance Board as though she had applied for the spouses' allowance. So she applies for the spouse's allowance, the war veterans allowance is cut off. So there is no change; the same number of dollars will be coming into the home.of this veteran of World War II and his wife.
But, she says to me, having seen certain things in the paper, what happens if her husband dies-his health is very poor- before she reaches 65? She is told she will lose everything. That is true. If he dies before she reaches 65, his old age security is dropped, his guaranteed income supplement is dropped, his 15 per cent disability pension dies with him because it is less than 48 per cent, and her spouse's allowance will be dropped because she is no longer a spouse but a widow.
The only thing I could say to her by way of hope was that in that circumstances, of course, she would be able to reapply for the allowance for a widow under the War Veterans Allowance Act. Nevertheless, she faces that prospect, and it is one, I suppose, that will probably happen, knowing her age and his health. What he is now getting will all drop because of the means test on the war veterans allowance and because of the marital test or the spouse's allowance.
Surely we can do better for a veteran who saw six years' service in World War II and who has suffered so much in the 30-odd years since then. Surely we can do a lot better for his wife and potential widow.
To do these things, the various pieces of legislation we spoke about need to be reconsidered and, in addition to what we should do about the Pension Act, the 48 per cent rule, the prisoners of war and so on, we now need a thorough overhaul of the War Veterans Allowance Act to make it come much closer to a guaranteed annual income for all our veterans. Mr. Speaker, I support the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure if the hon. member raised a point of order. I suggest he did not. Probably he did not understand my French, for which I am sorry. I have tried to explain my party's attitude to the minister and this bill.
Actually I am glad of the timing of this debate since it enables me to speak about certain things which concern me greatly. One of them is the urgent necessity for radar at Victoria international airport. I was not at all satisfied with the minister's reply to my questions on this subject. I asked two questions, on January 31 and again on February 16. One may read the minister's reply as reported on page 3097 of Hansard for February 16. Before I read the minister's answer perhaps I should explain what happened. On January 21 I took scheduled flight 266 from Victoria to Vancouver. An aircraft, not reported to the pilots of the scheduled airliner, almost collided with our aircraft. But for our pilot's evasive action, an accident would have happened. As I say, thanks to the speedy action of the captain of my particular aircraft, we avoided an

accident. In the face of this the minister had the gall to tell me that he had seen the report and I had grossly exaggerated what had happened. Frankly, I am not sure the minister saw the report. The report I hold in my hand mentions the imminence of a collision and says that if the captain had not taken evasive action the aircraft would have collided.
I had to accept the minister's explanation in the House. It was not a good explanation. I made inquiries, wanting to know what sort of report the minister had read, and was told by a variety of people that, since there had been no request for an inquiry, the incident was not considered as important. And that was the tone of the minister. I did not like his attempt to put me down, by suggesting it was not a serious incident. Perhaps he would like another by-election in Esquimalt-Saanich. I am not ready for that yet. At any rate, the minister's party would stand no chance of winning.
One part of the pilot's report refers to a near miss. I do not know if the minister was aware that another aircraft was in the air at the time. I had evidence of that aircraft's presence, as well. Soon after Air Canada flight 266 took off and had reached 2,000 feet, another aircraft was reported. That was cleared and there was no problem. The pilots of the small aircraft and the commercial airliner, each knew exactly where the other was, and that was fine. When the commercial airliner reached 3,500 feet of altitude, the pilot saw another aircraft, the one I spoke about earlier. We nearly collided with it. As I say, but for the rapid and appropriate evasive action taken by the captain of our aircraft, we would have collided.
I contest the minister's right to say that I grossly exaggerated the facts. The minister has his report, and I have mine. I know where the aircraft were, and I know they nearly collided. I wonder if the parliamentary secretary is prepared to table the report he is now waving in his hand.

To show you how important Victoria international airport is, let me put some statistics on record. Figures for November, 1976, show that Victoria international airport ranks thirteenth in the scale of total aircraft movements. There were some 13,600 take-offs and landings controlled by the control tower, as compared with some 15,000-odd at Vancouver airport. How many do you imagine there were at Mirabel? Would hon. members like to hear some statistics concerning Gander international airport? In my second question of February 16, I alluded to radar equipement being taken out of Vancouver airport. Let me point out how traffic at Victoria international airport has grown over the years. For example, in 1971 there were about 105,000 takeoffs and landings from Victoria. By 1975, according to the latest statistics I haved seen, the total had risen to 185,000. In 1971 there were about 135,000 take-offs and landings at Vancouver airport; by 1975 the figure had reached 203,000. Traffic at Ottawa international airport, on the other hand, declined from 219,000 movements in 1971 to 205,000 in 1975. That represents a drop of about 15 per cent. Movements at Victoria international rose from 105,000 to 185,000 in the same period. These figures are ample grounds for the case I have been trying to make in the past few months. I do not like being put down by an arrogant minister.
I received a letter which the minister did not even have the courtesy to sign. He got one of his flunkies, his executive assistant, to sign it. Presumably he wrote the letter. It reads in part:
I wish to assure you that flight safety in this area is not adversely affected by the unavailability of radar equipment. Effective pilot and air traffic control procedures are in use which are designed to give maximum assurance that the control tower staff at Victoria are aware of the position of all aircraft about to enter or operate within their area of responsibility.
This has been given the lie by that incident of January 21.1 am not yet sure whether the minister knows there were two aircraft as well as the commercial aircraft in the air at that time. My reports make it quite clear that there were. If that is not a hairy incident, I would like to know what is. Therefore I
National Transportation Act
feel it is time that I had a sensible, decorous and non-arrogant reply from the minister.
There are a couple of other tables I would like to record. Table 5 is related to the type of engine that is used when there is a distinction being made with regard to jets, turbo-props, and piston driven aircraft. There are itinerant movements, ones that are just going by. They are not the ones taking off and landing.
In the month of November there were some 6,000, of which 585 were jet take-offs and landings, 726 with turbo-props and 5,000 with piston engines. Anyone who has had anything whatsoever to do with flying knows that piston engines still do not travel as fast as jet aircraft. Their manner of getting out of the way or in the way is hampered by their speed.
In the incident to which I referred, it was the turbo driven aircraft that took the evasive action. It was quick to respond. The piston driven aircraft, which some of us, including myself, saw, seemed to be unaware of our presence.

speechtext: Were you scared?

speechtext:
I have had enough flying hours not to be scared. You get some flying hours in and you will understand.
At Gander, by comparison to the 6,480 total that I spoke of, there were only 1,600 of which 880 were jet, 200 turbo prop and 326 piston. This means there is a heavy concentration of piston driven aircraft in that particular area. It suggests to me there is every need for a radar at Victoria international airport. If the minister or his delightful parliamentary secretary, who had the courtesy to address me on one occasion, read this particular issue of Hansard, and want more information, I am quite prepared to give it.
There are two other matters. I am not sure whether time will permit me to deal with both. The first has to do with ferry subsidies. There has been a great deal of talk about the amount of subsidies provided to operate east coast ferries. Admittedly some of these subsidies must be provided constitutionally such as the ferry to Port aux Basques, Newfoundland. That subsidy is one of the terms of confederation with Newfoundland and the rest of Canada. The ferry between Prince Edward Island and the mainland is likewise an interprovincial ferry.
The argument we get from the other side of the House is that subsidies cannot be given in cases that are not interprovincial. If it is from one part of the province to the other part of the province, subsidies cannot be authorized. To that I say poppycock.
The Public Accounts of Canada will bear me out that there have been instances of subsidies granted to ferries, either for construction, operation, or slipways in which they berth at one end or the other of their passages, which operate within a single province. Two grants were made by the ministry to aid ferry vessel construction.
One grant of $3 million was made to the province of Ontario to aid in the construction of vessel and terminals for the
80010-30'/2

March 7, 1977
National Transportation Act
Tobermory-South Bay Mouth service. Reference to that service can be found in the Public Accounts of Canada 1973, page 26:12. I am not deploring this. I am glad it is there. 1 am happy to say that the design of the ferry operating on that service was perfected by naval designers in my constituency. It is something of which they are proud, and I am sure the people in the area are proud of it too.
The province of Quebec was granted $3 million to aid in the construction of an icebreaker type ferry for use on the St. Lawrence River. Reference to that may be found on the same page of the 1973 Public Accounts of Canada, 26 being Transport and 12 being the page within Transport. This was the ministry's share of a $6 million grant. The remaining $3 million was funded by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Therefore let us have no more of this hogwash from the other side about there being no subsidies available for ferries that are plying within provincial waters.
There is a very strong argument that needs to be put. It has been put by many of my colleagues on this side, and I am happy to say by some members opposite, that there is a need for a subsidy for the service of ferries on the west coast of the island.
There is one other matter that is of equal concern on the west coast. That is the passage of commercial and, particularly, tanker traffic in and out of the Straits of Juan de Fuca. This is a peculiar situation and I think it deserves some attention.
The Straits of Juan de Fuca separate Vancouver Island from the state of Washington, the Olympic Peninsula. It runs pretty well down the middle of the channel. There was one provision in the treaty under which that boundary was set. It makes it quite clear that all the waters south of the forty-ninth parallel-by the time it gets down to the Straits of Juan de Fuca it is south of the forty-ninth parallel-shall be free and open for navigation to the ships of both countries.
For navigational purposes, ships of both Canada and the United States may travel across the international boundary without getting into trouble with the coast guard, the police or whatever. They are not supposed to be doing any fishing. Let us not fool ourselves. It is navigation only.
A strange situation has developed within these waters between Vancouver Island and the Olympic Peninsula as far as the attitudes of the respective governments are concerned. On the Canadian side from the shoreline, the low water line of Vancouver Island, out to our midline which is our boundary, these are considered in Canada as internal waters; and as internal waters, international law, which includes the right of innocent passage, does not automatically apply. It may be granted on request, but not automatically.
On the American side of this boundary and down to the southern edge of it to the Olympic Peninsula, the first three miles off the low water line up toward the boundary are considered by the United States authorities as territorial waters. That is all, just three miles. From three miles to the international border, which in some places would be as much

as 12 and in some cases as little as 10, the United States authorities consider these waters as the high seas to which the right of innocent passage applies under international law. These are the waters into which the vessels carrying the crude oil from Prudhoe Bay should be entering, possibly before the end of the year. We have cause for concern.
There are two different regimes covering this body of water. In existence now is a voluntary system of pilotage. Ships coming in are expected to enter on the starboard side through waters which, under the U.S. interpretation, are the high seas and where they have the right to innocent passage. They are supposed to go out on the starboard side too, which puts them in Canadian waters where they do not have the right of innocent passage. This is a stupid situation. The Canadian and United States authorities must resolve it before the tankers come. One could imagine circumstances in which the standards on the Canadian side might be such that, having been allowed in by the American authorites, the vessels could not get out to sea again.
I do not know where the fault lies, but this situation must be sorted out because these are the waters in which the tankers carrying the crude oil will be sailing. Further, these are not calm waters. They are often subject to high winds, strong currents, fog. A voluntary system of traffic management will not do. We need something better. There must be a mandatory system in force from the Pacific Ocean through the Straits of Juan de Fuca to wherever these vessels go. I should like to see them prevented from coming in, because we have found a better place for them to offload their cargoes. But as matters now stand they are planning to come in, and I suggest everything possible be done to prepare for this in advance.
This afternoon the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Lee) was talking about the need to assist communities in coastal British Columbia with special reference to the services available to them by water. It was the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), urged on by some members of his own party, who was looking for some ways to save money-I hesitate to mention names but if pushed I might be able to produce one- who decided to go after the $4 million freight subsidy covering Northland Navigation.

speechtext: She got mad at him.
