speechtext:
Well, if she got mad at him at that time she might not have had quite as much influence as I thought she had. If she made a mistake, she backed away from it. People who live far from the coast do not understand about the need for a good freight and passenger transport service on that coast. This is a land of some 5,000 pioneers, we might call them, who are making their living in more than a hundred small, isolated communities from Howe Sound up to Rivers Inlet.
The coastline runs for 500 miles, encompassing some 150 inlets and places of call. One has to travel up that coast on one of these freight carriers to appreciate the beauty and also the
March 7, 1977

danger of the voyage, not to mention the need for this service. Those who use it are Indian reserves, logging camps, stores, sawmills, fishing camps, guides, summer resorts and retirement communities ranging from one or two families to 250 people. There is no other way of reaching these places unless by a privately-owned float plane. What do these vessels carry? They carry explosives, food, furniture, compressed gas. And liquor. I have seen them onloading the empties-not on this coast but on the west coast of Vancouver Island-and offloading the full bottles from the provincial liquor board. They carry livestock, lumber, machinery, tires, trucks and wire rope. They also bring cargo to the Vancouver market, shakes and shingles, machinery for repair, frozen shrimps, and sometimes even dirty laundry.
Aircraft have been suggested as a supplementary means of transport in the area. But aircraft are hampered by seasonal conditions, fog most of all. In the long haul sea transport provides the only communication with the outside world for weeks and weeks. This is the area from which the subsidy has been withdrawn, throwing the communities north of Vancouver into a complete tizzy. I trust that other members of the House, both on this side and across the way, will be addressing themselves to this particular matter. These are not ferries about which I have been talking.
Ferries join the mainland to Vancouver Island, both to Nanaimo and to Schwartz Bay in my riding. Fares on these services have had to be doubled in the last year to make them pay. The route from Nanaimo to Horseshoe Bay is part of the trans-Canada highway. That highway was built with subsidies from federal funds. I just cannot understand why there is a gap in the trans-Canada highway because no subsidy has been paid, as it has on other parts, both for maintenance and construction. The slipway also deserves a subsidy, as do the vessels themselves and the vessel operations.
I see Your Honour is getting a little unsettled, so with that I will say thank you very much.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome Bill C-33. I feel it is a piece of legislation which is going to put back into law what has, in effect, been the practice regarding the government's relationship with the Canadian Transport Commission. The so-called independence of that commission which was touted when the existing legislation was passed about ten years ago never really materialized, and in many instances-I intend to give an example of one later-it was actually used to camouflage, in effect, the government's own unwillingness to take certain steps. This legislation brings back to the cabinet full responsibility, which in effect was always there anyway but which was at times at least partially camouflaged. The legislation is a needed rationalization. I am looking forward to supporting the bill in committee and perhaps trying to improve certain aspects of it.
The subject matter to which I wish to address myself tonight is urban transit. The House had an opportunity to discuss urban transit last Friday but the debate was a fairly one-sided
National Transportation Act
affair so far as this side of the House was concerned. It was a very good example of just how the political perception of members of this House as to what policies are vital to the well being of this country can be affected by home town or home constituency realities.
With the exception of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Kaplan), who addressed himself to two arguments against the government's living up to the promises it made to the Canadian public during the 1974 election campaign, the fact that no other member from an urban riding had the opportunity to speak, on this side, is an indication that, although we got the rural view, we did not get the point of view of members who every day are under the gun from their electorate in regard to what is going to happen next to relieve the almost unbearable conditions many of them have to put up with going back and forth to work because, for a number of reasons, they live in areas of the country which are not served by public transit facilities.
It is all very well to say that this is a provincial matter. It is all very well to say, as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance said, that there have been two major fundamental changes in Canada since the 1974 election. Double digit inflation and the need for restraint have become paramount in the government's considerations regarding embarking upon new programs. The parliamentary secretary's other argument was that since November 15 last the prospect is for a major realignement in the federal-provincial division of powers. I do not know that he used that exact term, but in any event he implied that this was a very poor time for the federal government to be launching new spending programs in areas where there is a fairly clear provincial responsibility.
The two arguments that he made, he made well, but I feel that the counter arguments-I will advance at least half a dozen of the major ones-far outweigh whatever merit or validity the two positions that he advanced had.
As for double digit inflation and the restraint program, surely, Mr. Speaker, we are facing in this country a situation where, unless something is done quickly about our energy consumption and unless something is done soon to move away from the tremendous reliance on petroleum product consumption, we will find ourselves in an extremely dangerous financial position vis-a-vis our balance of payments and our trade picture with the rest of the world.
The energy conservation aspect is only one part of the total picture in terms of petroleum product consumption. An urban transit program can be started now but it will be two or three years down the road before any serious demands for money are going to be made. The total cost for the economy over the medium term, say 12 to 15 years, will be tremendous unless a program is commenced now. The potential for gasoline savings by moving quickly to public transit in our urban areas and major cities and suburbs is enormous. Moving over the longer haul to electrical transportation systems using rails has even greater energy conservation potential.
As for the prospect which the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance fears, namely, a realignment of feder-

March 7, 1977
National Transportation Act
al-provincial powers, I do not feel like jumping the gun on that subject now. From what I can see the public of Canada is still largely sympathetic to a strong central government acting where there is a need and a reasonable case for federal intervention and where there is some constitutional responsibility.
In the area of urban transit there are several constitutional grounds which I would argue justify federal intervention. There is a clearcut federal responsibility for railways and I would suggest that as the promise in 1974 included action on public transit systems involving the use of rail facilities, passenger train facilities, as well as railroad beds being upgraded for rapid transit use, these are all matters where constitutionally the federal government can and should have an input.
When I refer, as I did earlier, to the whole question of energy conservation and the long-term effect this can have on the balance of payments and the future economic prosperity of this country, then it seems to me we have a constitutional responsibility above and beyond our responsibility with regard to railways. This does and should allow us to provide at least the kind of catalystic funding which could stimulate the public transit programs which this country, and particularly the suburbs which have grown up around the cities, so desperately need.
What is happening now is unfortunately reminiscent of what happened with our entire housing program after the Second World War. In the early 1950's the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was established. The intention was that it would not only provide good housing for Canadians-which it did eventually by establishing standards which make Canadians today well housed in comparison with any other country and we can be proud of it-but at the beginning it had another hope just as important as housing. It was concerned that the places where houses were to be built should be well planned. The idea was to use the lending power of CMHC to require the municipalities and the provinces where the housing was to be built, to plan properly.
Unfortunately the Liberal government of the day in its wisdom did not want to go out on a limb. It felt that it could not do this constitutionally so in effect all this housing, with a few exceptions, was built at the whim of local developers and local municipal politicians were the arbiters. In my view this was a tragedy. We had the power at that time to develop suburbs that made sense from every point of view.
Recently members of this House who sit on the committee for the National Capital Region attended a seminar arranged by the Parliamentary Centre for Foreign Relations in Washington, D.C. where they had an opportunity to visit Columbia, one of the new cities that lies outside Washington. I also had had an opportunity previously to visit Reston. These are two new cities planned from scratch and they could have been emulated in this country. Back in the 1950's we had the people, the architects, and the visionary planners to do this but they were not allowed to.
[Mr. Watson.)
Let me give an example of what can happen with this kind of planning. Neighbourhoods are arranged around schools, then there are villages made up of several neighbourhoods and sufficient villages in the case of Columbia to make a city of about 100,000 people. The result is that 85 per cent of the children can walk to school. In Columbia alone this year school busing costs show a saving of over $1 million. It is estimated that the saving in school bus and transportation related capital investment is $150 million compared to what it would have been if there had been no planning.
This is only one aspect of the potential saving through this type of planning. We had the potential to do it and failed. We still have not influenced planning concepts in the development of almost all our suburbs.
I suggest that we are in the process of doing the same thing with urban transit funds as we did with housing. The Railway Relocation and Crossing Act passed in 1974 not only provides for upgrading of existing rail lines for rapid transit purposes but more important, it provides as a precondition of federal funding of a rapid transit or public transit plan or regional transportation plan that there be a regional development plan. Section 3(1) of the act reads as follows:
Where, in respect of an area in a province that includes or comprises an urban area (hereinafter in this Part called a "transportation study area"), the government of the province and all the municipalities within that area have agreed upon an urban development plan and transportation plan (hereinafter in this Part called an "accepted plan") for that transportation study area, the province or a municipality may, subject to subsection (5), apply to the Commission for such orders as the Commission may make under section 6 and as arc necessary to carry out the accepted plan.
The railway relocation plan which we passed in April of 1974 is the framework for making full use of our railway lines around cities or for public transit purposes, and it also-and this is the portion which is so important-provides that prior to doing this there must be not only agreement with the provinces but a regional transport plan and a regional development plan. These requirements would mean that in the future at least we will avoid the kind of development lacking public transit facilities which have characterized our surburban growth since World War II. If we do not move quickly toward funding urban transit, we will be making the same mistake for which we are now paying the consequences in excessive automobile use and excessive reliance on the automobile.
I mentioned our constitutional rights regarding railways and 1 have made reference to energy self-sufficiency obviously being a national objective. Surely the quality of living of our people is a matter of concern. In my own district of Laprairie-Chateauguay there are people who leave their houses at 6.30 in the morning in order to be at work or in class at 9 a.m., and yet they are only 15 miles away from their offices or classes. They have to put in an hour and a half of waiting in line to get across a bridge which is crowded with automobile traffic. Almost all the people trying to cross the bridge in the morning had moved into the area into houses built with CMHC loans or guarantees. It is we who have lent them money in a totally unplanned way.
March 7, 1977

We encouraged development in these areas through CMHC. Now we are standing back and washing our hands of the responsibility. Not only on the south and north shores of Montreal but across the country until three or four years ago the development that took place was largely funded by CMHC direct loans or CMHC guarantees. We encouraged these people to move into the suburbs, and now we wash our hands of them.
The example which the United States is giving us in the area of conservation will be brought home very effectively to us when President Carter next April 20 makes his announcement. We have been footdraggging on the question of energy conservation and we will have to be prepared to accept large increases in our fuel costs, restrictions on the kinds of automobiles we drive and the kinds of luxuries we enjoy if we are serious about energy conservation.
Last summer Gallup made a poll of the Canadian population on the subject of the desirability of increased conservation efforts in the nation. Of the respondents, 85.8 per cent said that it was desirable to have increased conservation efforts, 9.1 per cent said no, and 5.1 per cent had no opinion. Surely to those members of the government who accord some importance to public opinon polls this poll should be fairly convincing.
While I do not expect us to move to the federal U.S. position which involved the U.S. government paying 80 per cent of urban transit systems across the United States as well as a percentage of the operating costs, it seems to me that the formulas which were outlined during the 1974 campaign, most of which involved a 50 per cent sharing of costs, make a lot of sense. They made sense then, they were good promises, promises which at that time the government obviously felt it could back up. Rather than as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance has said, that there are two major reasons why we should not fulfill these promises, 1 would argue that the reverse is true. If anything has happened, the factors which would make such a program more essential now than ever have become increasingly evident. Energy conservation is one, and world costs of petroleum which have gone up considerably even since 1974 are another.
I have mentioned conservation, living standards, and the quality of living to which surely we have to pay some attention. If you have people waiting in line at bridges crossing to the island of Montreal, crossing into Vancouver or coming into one of the Toronto expressways every morning for minutes or sometimes hours on end, this is a waste not only of energy but of human resources which is unacceptable in a society which prides itself on wishing to give us all a better quality of life.
The absolutely startling figures which were revealed last year when the budget estimates were tabled for 1975-76 indicated an overwhelming expenditure of federal funds to even out petroleum prices for all Canadians. We had to spend a total $1.6 billion to even out the price to all Canadians to make up the difference between the world price which we paid for petroleum for our eastern market and which was sold at the much lower domestic price and what we were not able to
National Transportation Act
cover of that world and domestic differential from our sales of petroleum to the United States at world prices. I think it would be a fairly reasonable guess-although I do not pretend it to be accurate-that of that $1.6 billion, $800 million went on gasoline expenditure. We spent that year approximately $800 million out of our budget to subsidize the consumption of gasoline in this country. We then felt it necessary to institute-as we did in 1975-a ten cents a gallon gasoline tax which helped to reduce that tremendous drain on our federal resources.
With this ten cents per gallon gasoline tax I understand our gasoline now sells at very close to the world price, but I argue that if it really does boil down to a question of finding funds and not being able to find them anywhere else, that we should direct our attention to that ten cents per gallon tax and use it, even if it means we have to bring the price of gasoline up to the world price and have the ten cents per gallon added to that world price. It should be used to fund what we have to do in the area of urban transit, and if there is anything left over it should be used for other conservation efforts. That would bring the price of gasoline above the world price, but it would allow us to continue to keep the price of heating oil slightly under the world price. This is the kind of hard decision which 1 feel the government is going to have to make if it expects to receive the confidence of the Canadian public in the future.
I never cease to be puzzled by the shortsighted arguments which are advanced against urban transit funding by the government. When we desire to create new jobs in high technology fields-and half a dozen ministers are talking about this continually-surely this is a suitable endeavour in the Montreal area, in the Thunder Bay, Winnipeg and Toronto areas.
There are several major companies and literally dozens of subsidiary companies which would be affected by the side effects of a major move into the building of urban transit vehicles of one kind or another in this country. This is the kind of job creating program which really does make sense. It makes far more sense than some of the nonsensical efforts we seem to make from time to time to stimulate job development in various parts of the country.
A measure which was, in effect, ready to be legislated was the proposed transport development corporation. It was all set to go. It was drafted, but it has been held back and never brought before this House by way of legislation. The advantages of standardization across the country in urban transit systems are so obvious that there should not even be an argument. These things have all been left to linger or drag along. They have not been pushed, and it comes back to what I said at the very beginning. It is unfortunate, but the perspective of the people in this House is determined by their own constituency needs. For example, if the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) were sitting for the South Shore instead of for the town of Mount Royal, and if he did not have a train running through a tunnel from the middle of the city to his riding, hon.

March 7, 1977
National Transportation Act
members could be sure that he would have a different perspective.
If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) did not represent a downtown area and instead was representing an area like mine where his constituents were knocking on his door and telephoning him about the problem, he would have a different perspective. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) has a potential transit vehicle company in his constituency. It is an important transit vechicle company, and perhaps he should have another look at that aspect of the urban transit problem.
There is another important need which hon. members should not ignore when they are thinking about influencing the future relationship between the people of Canada and the federal government. Are we at the federal level going to be a completely foreign element as far as the average man in the street is concerned henceforth in this new federal-provincial relationship which the parliamentary secretary thinks is about to evolve, as he mentioned last Friday? Are we simply going to have a very remote relationship with the public? If that is the case, I really do not think the future looks very good for the federal government. When it can do so constitutionally the federal government needs to be in close contact with the public. By satisfying a public need which has been demonstrated in all the major cities of this country and in the suburbs of those cities for the last 15 years surely we bring ourselves closer to the people.
This closeness with the people is surely one of the stronger arguments members of the cabinet should be considering when contemplating whether they should spend the extra funds to which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) alluded briefly in his remarks last Friday. I can only appeal to the cabinet that the time has come to make a favourable decision with regard to an expanded urban transit program and to the proposed transport development corporation to encourage the new technology which can produce, with Canadian effectiveness, not only adequate vehicles to service our cities in the field of urban transit for the next 15, 20 or 30 years but which can provide jobs and a fantastic amount of export market potential as well.
There are so many good arguments in favour of this that I really cannot fathom why the obviousness of the case has yet to convince the powers that be, and especially the financial powers that be, who somehow feel that the program of restraint has to zero in on a program like this one, which makes sense from every conceivable point of view, including the financial point of view. If only they would stand back from their desk, look out the window, and just think a little bit about the future of Canada-surely this is something we can ask them to do-and if they take a few minutes and apply a little Canadian common sense to this situation, then they will sympathetically review and fulfil the promises which they so generously made in the spring of 1974.
The optimism which engendered those promises surely is no less justified now, and I hope we can hear some encouragement from them in the next few days. The budget is coming

out on March 31. It must contain much more than we have been led to anticipate so far by the Minister of Finance.

speakeroldname: Mr. Janies A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great attention to the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I want to congratulate the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) on what I consider to be a very well reasoned, well thought out, and well presented speech. Having sat on his side of the House in a position not dissimilar to his, I know from experience how difficult it was for him to make a speech like that. However, surely that is the kind of speech which has to be made from time to time to keep reminding the government of commitments it made and the moral obligation it has to discharge these commitments.
Naturally we were appalled, to say the least, when we heard the statement issued by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in Toronto a short time ago. He declared that the government would not be able to discharge its commitment to spend $290 million on assisting urban areas meet their transit responsibilities to commuters. The government made that promise in 1974, as part of its election platform. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) emphasized it in a speech in Winnipeg. Two years after making the promise, the government, forced into austerity by the need to restrain federal spending, announced it could not keep that commitment.
Even though large municipalities, including metropolitan Toronto, metropolitan Winnipeg and Montreal had either begun planning how to take advantage of the federal urban transit commitment or had already spent substantial sums on programs in which it was thought the federal government would participate, the government announced it could not fulfil its commitment. I say the government will change its mind, must change it, indeed shall change it, given the economic climate in this country. I suspect that in his budget speech on March 31 the Minister of Finance will announce that the government knows how necessary is the commitment with respect to urban transit it made in 1974 to the cities. The government must also feel a moral obligation to its members representing urban areas for, to a large extent, many of them were elected, or re-elected as the case may be, on the basis of the program the government presented to the people of Canada in that campaign. The hon. member for Laprairie and other urban members documented their concern in the debate last Friday and in the questions they have raised in this house.
Despite the fine print in the Constitution, the federal government has become increasingly involved in matters under provincial jurisdiction. It has become increasingly involved in urban problems, and its responsibility for helping our growing cities is just as great as if it were clearly spelled out in the Constitution. That commitment grew from the federal government's involvement in housing. Many years ago it passed the National Housing Act, which was originally envisaged as a means of funding housing, and established Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation as the executive arm to implement the provisions of the National Housing Act.
March 7, 1977

Once the federal government became so greatly involved in housing, an area which had been clearly under provincial jurisdiction, it had the concomitant responsibility to assist in planning. That responsibility carried with it the commitment to assist with urban transit, in other words, the responsibility to make sure that our cities were planned in such a way that those who lived on the fringes, in the suburbs, would have adequate transit facilities for travelling to and from their places of work. That commitment is even more important today, considering it is estimated that by the turn of the, century more than half our population will live in the three large metropolitan areas, greater Montreal, metropolitan Toronto, and the greater Vancouver area. In addition, we must provide for the growth of our medium-sized cities. This responsibility entails the provision of efficient means of transport to ensure that growth is orderly and that people who are obliged to live in our growing suburban areas will have adequate and equal access to their places of employment and business.
The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) and municipal and other authorities in Canada have tried to reach a trilevel consensus which would make it possible for the federal jurisdiction to deal directly with the municipalities, in order to assist them in their ongoing and ever growing commitments. That is only as it should be, considering that the British North America Act does not provide our municipalities with adequate tax resources for discharging their commitments, whereas, paradoxically, at the other end of the scale the Government of Canada takes in more money than it needs.
I hope that the federal government will, as the Prime Minister has already suggested, re-assess and re-examine its position. In that regard I look forward to hearing the Minister of Finance make his budget speech on March 31.
The House passed the National Transportation Act almost ten years ago and this is our first opportunity since passage of that law to examine the policies which the National Transportation Act created and to look closely at the Canadian Transport Commission, the main regulatory agency established under the act. Of course we are also examining various transportation agencies in the country, especially the two major railways. If my memory serves me right, we have not been able to examine in committee the annual report of Canadian National Railways for at least four or five years. That makes it all the more important to raise the subject in the present debate on second reading of Bill C-33.
I come from a province which relies heavily on the federal transport commitment. It is crucial to the economy of the Atlantic provinces, and vital to the economy of Newfoundland. For us, an ongoing transportation commitment is essential. It is essential for the Government of Canada to spell out its contractual obligation to the province of Newfoundland, an obligation to assist economic growth by taking a major role in transportation to and from, and within Newfoundland. Until 1969 the major ground transport system in Newfoundland consisted of a train service operated by Canadian National Railways. As the result of a decision of the Canadian Trans-
National Transportation Act
port Commission in 1968, this service ceased on April 15, 1969.
The Canadian Transport Commission directed that, in place of the train service, a cross-island bus service should operate within the province of Newfoundland. That is contained in the Canadian Transport Commission's order No. R2673 of July, 1968. I quote it for the record:
The bus service proposed by the Applicants and described in detail in the Judgment of Woodard, C., shall be inaugurated and continued as long as a requirement for passenger service continues, and the passenger facilities, including terminals and the shelters mentioned therein, with proper communication links, shall be provided and installed, all to the satisfaction of the Committee.
That directive by the Canadian Transport Commission was carried out by CN up to July, 1976. As a result of an application which CN made to the Public Utilities Board of the province of Newfoundland for an increase in fares and as a result of a jurisdictional dispute which flowed from that application, CN, notwithstanding the fact that the Supreme Court of Canada had ruled that the Public Utilities Board had jurisdiction by virtue of Part III of the National Transportation Act not having been proclaimed, withdrew its bus service on July 12, 1976. That was a violation of a directive by a quasi-judicial body acting under the statutory authority of the Newfoundland legislature.
What we found incomprehensible was the attitude of the Government of Canada. We appealed to the Government of Canada. The premier of the province sent a wire to the Prime Minister on July 15 last year. We set out the legal obligation of Canadian National vis-a-vis the Public Utilities Board of Newfoundland as determined by the ruling of the Supreme Court of Canada. The premier set out in the wire the constitutional obligation with regard to the Terms of Union and the order of the Canadian Transport Commission which 1 quoted, that CN continue to provide a bus service within the province.
That appeal was made to the Prime Minister to direct this Crown corporation to obey the laws of the province of Newfoundland. That is all we were asking, that they restore the service on which the people of Newfoundland were wholly dependent.
Instead of the Prime Minister acting in a responsible way and directing, by order in council, that CN restore that service in pursuance of the directive of the Canadian Transport Commission, an order in council was passed the following day, July 16, at the instance of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), placing the CN road cruiser service in the province of Newfoundland under the National Transportation Act.
Nobody questions the right of the Government of Canada to proclaim that section of the act and place that particular service under it. However, surely it would have been logical to assume that before that was done the service would be restored under its existing jurisdiction, and that the laws of the province of Newfoundland as set out by the Public Utilities Board in its ruling would be upheld.

March 7, 1977
National Transportation Act
What was at issue was an application by CN for a fare increase of up to 150 per cent. Our Public Utilities Board had the nerve and the gall to say they could only have an increase of up to 30 per cent, that this in fact could not be justified on a user pay basis. They stated that it was a part of the national rail service of this country and that, to all intents and purposes, the CN road cruiser service in the province of Newfoundland, since it had a monopoly on ground transportation in the province, had the same function as CN trains before they ceased to operate in 1969.
The dispute was never resolved, the Supreme Court of Canada notwithstanding and the Constitution notwithstanding. Instead, we had an order in council passed placing the CN road cruiser service under the National Transportation Act.
The next episode in this unsavory story was an application, which we knew would follow very soon, by CN to the Canadian Transport Commission for an increase in rates. That application is now before the commission. It is very interesting because it tells it all. They modified their demands to the point where the application now before the Canadian Transport Commission calls for only an 8 per cent fare increase. However, they state, and this concerns us in the province of Newfoundland, that they are placing the service on a user pay concept. That is completely contrary to the spirit, intent and letter of the policy now before us.
In this regard I wish to quote the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) when introducing this bill on March 1. I quote from page 3525 of Hansard'.
There arc, and probably will always be, some services which are required in order to meet legitimate economic and social needs such as regional development or access to remote communities but for which the particular users cannot reasonably be expected to pay the full costs.
I tried to establish that that is obviously the case up to this point in time with regard to the CN road cruiser service in Newfoundland. The minister went on to say:
In such cases government support in the form of direct or indirect subsidy is necessary and reasonable. Government support of this kind to ensure the provision of necessary transportation facilities which cannot be commercially viable represents the use of transportation as an instrument for the achievement of economic and social objectives.
In further support of my contention I wish to quote from the June 18, 1974, Prime Minister's announcement, "Liberal party program on transportation, inter-city passenger transportation". I quote:
The Passenger Transport Corporation-
That is a corporation which the government promised to set up in 1974.
-will also ensure, with provincial co-operation, high quality passenger bus services in areas not adequately served by existing carriers.
The Prime Minister went on to refer to a "super-bus" service. We would be satisfied with ordinary bus service if we could be assured that bus service would be a part of the national transportation grid in Canada, that it would be treated the same as the new VIA rail passenger service which the minister announced, and that it would qualify in the same way for whatever federal government subsidies there may be.
(Mr. McGrath.]
This would enable the CN to provide a level of service in the province of Newfoundland in accordance with the national transportation policy. This super-bus service was to be introduced between medium-sized centres. Fares on these buses would be reasonable, but vastly superior terminal and on-board comfort and services would be provided.
I only wish the Minister of Transport and some of his officials could go to Newfoundland and take the present CN bus service from St. John's to Port aux Basques. It is the only way our people can travel across the province unless they go by air from Halifax. Let the minister take the road cruiser service, as it is referred to by the CN, from Port aux Basques to St. John's across the trans-Canada Highway, which is 600 miles long and well below ordinary trans-Canada standards; indeed it is beginning to show substantial wear and tear as a result of CN truck traffic, something which in itself is a major cause of concern. The minister and his officials should take that 14 or 15 hour trip across that long and, in many places, desolate stretch of highway. They would then realize what our people have to go through.
There are no adequate terminal facilities. There are no adequate facilities en route. People are unable to buy meals because satisfactory facilities are not available at designated stops within the time allotted for the stop-overs. In many cases there are no shelters at places where people have to stand to wait for these buses. Once aboard, passengers have to sit in fairly cramped quarters. All too often they are able to find standing room only. I really wish the minister and his officials could take that trip.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: The scenery is very picturesque, though.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
The hon. member says it is very picturesque. I suggest that regardless of how picturesque the scenery might be he would soon get tired of a most uncomfortable ride under most unsatisfactory conditions.
I have described what it is like to take that journey in the hope that hon. members will realize it is the only means of travel we have in Newfoundland, and I should like some assurance from the minister before this bill passes that the CN bus service in the province of Newfoundland, or in any other province in which the railways intend to operate such a service, will be considered within the terms of the Prime Minister's statement that where they fulfil the same need as railways they will be able to qualify for whatever federal subsidies there are as part of the government's transportation policies.
A short time ago the Minister of Transport met with the three maritime premiers and the minister of transport for the province of Newfoundland. I must say I was encouraged by the new attitude exemplified in the press release from the Department of Transport on the outcome of that conference. I quote from that communique of February 8, 1977.
Mr. Lang, Mr. Morgan and the Maritime Premiers agreed in principle that improved passenger transportation could best be achieved by providing special assistance for upgrading bus and air services in the region.
March 7, 1977

Hon. members will note that they were not specific. The problem with which we have to contend in Newfoundland is that the CN enjoys a monopoly. There is only one bus service throughout the province, whereas in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, while still having the advantage of rail passenger service, passengers can choose between several other modes of ground transportation which are competing for their dollars.
Anyway, if that communique is an indication of the minister's new policy, I wish he would tell us what his position is before the CTC brings down a decision with regard to the application by CN for what is to be the first of several anticipated increases in the fares to be charged on the road cruiser service in Newfoundland. 1 intend to press him on this matter when the bill goes to committee, and to do so again in the House should I have an opportunity. 1 ask the minister to tell us what he has in mind because this is most relevant to whatever decision is reached by the CTC with respect to the application by the CN for further increases in fares.
I should like some assurance that in addition to improvements in the service-and, God knows, there is an obvious need for improvements-there will be an improvement in the support services, for example, the installation of adequate terminal facilities across the province, and scheduling which will ensure that enough space is available to cope with peak periods-I have in mind holiday times, and co-ordination with the semesters of universities and colleges.
The minister has taken an obligation upon himself. We intend to hold him to it. He did so by virtue of the order in council passed last July which placed his imprimatur upon an illegal act committed by the CN. That is what it was. The minister gave an illegal act his imprimatur when he had the order in council passed removing jurisdiction from the Newfoundland Public Utilities Board and placing it under the authority of the CTC by virtue of the National Transportation Act. I hope that now he has the responsibility, notwithstanding how long the CTC may take before making a decision on the present application, a directive will be issued with respect to the obvious need for the improvement of the service in my province.
It always intrigues me that there should be no CN bus service to handle passengers coming ashore from the east coast ferry which operates between North Sydney and Argentia. Passengers using this ferry depend on private transport, which is not always adequate. Indeed it is not always available. It seems logical to me to expect that the CN, which operates this ferry service, would be able to direct one of its road cruisers to meet the ferry when it arrives.
There should also be some rescheduling of the bus service to fit in with airline schedules so that we could co-ordinate the total pattern of travel within and outside the province more effectively.
We have had to depend on CN in our province for a long time. I assume that, notwithstanding the new Via rail service and the new corporation which is to handle rail passenger service, we shall still have to depend on the CN for some time
National Transportation Act
to come to fulfil the major part of our passenger and freight traffic requirements.
Now we are going to have another study, a royal commission, which is about to be established to examine the transportation picture in the province of Newfoundland. The initiative for this study did not come from the Government of Canada or from the government of Newfoundland; the initiative came from Canadian National. Of course it found a willing participant in the federal government in the Minister of Transport, and so the study is going to be a joint study.
I regret very much that the province of Newfoundland has agreed to this study, because it is only two years since we had the last study, known as the trans-Newfoundland corridor transportation study. There are 11 volumes to that study, Mr. Speaker, which was commissioned in 1972 by the Canadian Transport Commission under the direction of the then minister of transport. It released its report in March of 1974. The study cost the people of Canada $370,000, and not one of the conclusions reached or recommendations made by that study has been acted upon to this day.
Surely it is only reasonable to ask, before we embark upon another study, just what exactly is the government's position vis-a-vis the findings, conclusions, and recommendations of this last study. Or could it be that this new royal commission is merely a means, a traditional Canadian means if you like, of shelving the problem so that we do not have to deal with it for a while-so we can put the problem into cold storage for the next two or three years? We have already been postponing major decisions for two or three years since we had the last study. We are now to have another royal commission, which I suppose will cost another $500,000 or more, to bring in some further recommendations in another two years, when another government will be in office. Then another royal commission could put the thing on ice for another two years.
There is a limit to our patience, Mr. Speaker; obviously there has to be. Ours is a vast province with a relatively small population. We must have an efficient transportation system in the province, both passenger and freight, to ensure that there is economic growth within the province. Economic growth in our province in becoming crucial in these days in view of the rate of unemployment in Newfoundland today, which I believe is around 25 per cent.
I suppose there is not much more I can say about the new study; we are going to have it anyway. The Newfoundland government has agreed to it, and so has the Minister of Transport. It is just a matter now of making the announcement, and I expect that will be made any day now. I hope that one of the first things the royal commission does when it receives its commission will be to examine the 11 volumes of the trans-Newfoundland corridor transportation study commissioned by the Canadian Transport Commission and undertaken by the firm of Messrs. Peat, Marwick and Company. Certainly this is more than the Government of Canada has

March 7, 1977
Adjournment Debate
done, because to this day not one of the findings or recommendations made in that report has been acted upon.
Before resuming my seat, may I say to the Minister of Transport, albeit in his absence, that before this debate is concluded we hope he will speak, notwithstanding the fact that his colleague, the Minister of Justice introduced the second reading debate on this bill. We hope he will address himself to the matters that have been raised during the course of this debate. I should like to hear him respond to the very eloquent, well reasoned, and well documented case put by the hon. member for Laprairie who preceded me in this debate. 1 hope he will have something to say to the people of Newfoundland who are beginning to feel they have been canned by these studies, and who certainly are feeling they have been studied to death by this government.

subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-POSITION OF CMHC ON USE OF ALUMINUM WIRING IN DWELLINGS
CONSUMER AFFAIRS-POSITION OF CMHC ON USE OF ALUMINUM WIRING IN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day I asked the minister responsible for housing whether he would consider recommending that any building constructed under federal auspices should have the same protection which any federal public works has. As 1 pointed out privately to the minister at the time, the department has said that when it is constructing any building under the auspices of the federal government-there are a large number built each year-it is a requirement of the tender that no aluminum wiring be used, or at least that only copper wiring be used. Mr. Bowen, the departmental official concerned, indicated that so far to his knowledge no such building has been built since this instruction was sent out under the federal tendering system. It seems to me that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should do no less.
It is the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) whose responsibility really this is. I have a bill recommending a ban on the use of aluminum wiring in domestic housing. The minister has said there is nothing wrong with
[Mr. McGrath.)
aluminum wiring, and he is correct, Mr. Speaker; there is absolutely nothing wrong with aluminum wiring so long as you do not hook it up to a power source. But normally you hook it up to a power source, which connects it to the circuitry in a house, and this is where the problem lies.
Two things happen with aluminum wiring which do not happen so readily with copper wiring. First of all, with aluminum wiring when you scratch the bright, shiny aluminum the shininess disappears and oxidation takes place almost instantaneously. When it becomes oxidized it, in effect, insulates against the proper conduct of electricity. When aluminum wires are bent over for the purpose of screwing them into switches or receptacles in the wall, the exposed wiring again almost immediately oxidizes.
Secondly, heat affects the expansion of aluminum many times faster than with copper. If you have copper screws in your receptacle and heat develops, as it will due to weakness in aluminum wiring caused by the oxidation, the aluminum wire passing around the screw will expand. This in effect flattens the wire because it then cannot expand beyond the allowance of the screw. When the wire cools, it is no longer directly connected but there is a gap. It also oxidizes where the flattening has taken place.
There are 500,000 homes with aluminum wiring in this country. I could point out the decisions that have been made in the United States and what has been done about it there, but we do not have to talk about that; what we should talk about is what we are going to do to protect people in Canada. Hydro authorities have stated that if the wiring is properly installed it is not dangerous, and that is true. Proper installation would mean adding a piece on the end of the aluminum wire. After it was cleaned a clip would be put over the wire. There would be pentrox grease inside the clip. A hydraulic clamp would then be squeezed firmly in place. The clamp would likely be made of copper so the process would be expensive. But, Mr. Speaker, it will have to happen.
One of the major culprits in this town that has looked for a shortcut at the risk of human life is the Campeau Corporation in the subdivisions it has developed. It is interesting to note that when Mr. Campeau's own house burned down there was some indication that the fire was caused by the electrical wiring system-aluminum wiring apparently. It can be argued whether or not that was so. But he built a new $150,000 house and used aluminum wiring in it. The television cameras were there to watch the installation which was widely publicized. And why was that? Because even at the risk of his own life and his children's lives he had to establish credibility so that he would not lose his money through having to rewire the Campeau subdivisions.
I am positive one little girl was lost in a subdivision fire in Ottawa last year because of electrical wiring, and I am pretty sure there were two more boys burned in the same subdivision shortly afterwards. People expert in the field say that the main problem will not develop for ten years.
March 7, 1977

I suggest that we outlaw the use of aluminum wiring in future building and tag all houses that now have it so that people will know it is there and that a dangerous situation exists.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the important question raised by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) prompted some inquiries on my part not only within the ministry but in my own files. I was familiar with the question mainly because a member on this side of the House, the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik), had spoken to me several times during the last year about aluminum wiring. I found in my files several documents, not the least of them a memorandum written by the hon. member for Ontario on June 10, 1976, and addressed to several ministers. Knowing the hon. member for Ontario I am sure he will be flattered at the interest being shown in his cause by the hon. member for Timiskaming.
The matter of the installation of aluminum wiring was examined by a task force on aluminum terminations. This task force, set up under the auspices of the Canadian Standards Association, agreed that the new terminal devices which have been introduced are satisfactory but that a standard for aluminum wire should be developed to ensure that an acceptable and consistent product continues to be acceptable.
Provincial authorities, having the responsibility for establishing and enforcing electrical wiring safety standards, have taken steps to overcome initial inadequacies in the connecting devices and workmanship. They appear to be actively reviewing the matter and displaying a readiness to take any further action necessary to ensure that aluminum wiring installation will be adequately controlled and will meet acceptable standards.
Subject to new factors or changes in present conditions, we believe that this matter must be resolved by those agencies which have the expertise in the electrical field and which have been entrusted with responsibility for safety in electrical installations.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-STATEMENT OF MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT'S ACCOMMODATION OF LABOUR-GOVERNMENT POSITION
LABOUR CONDITIONS-STATEMENT OF MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT'S ACCOMMODATION OF LABOUR-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to remind the House that in a speech made on October 28, 1976, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) said:
One of the first things we want to do is to create a national forum which would discuss and make recommendations on the big economic issues of the day. Such a forum would bring together representatives of government, labour, business, the farm community, possibly others.
In that speech he also said:
This is a program I have been developing with my departmental officials over several months. I will not be deterred by inflation. I will not be deterred by the wage and price control program, or by labour's opposition to it, or by opposition in the business community to the restraints.
Adjournment Debate
That was the minister's position setting out government policy on October 28.
On November 27 last, as reported at page 1332 of Hansard,
I asked about the other parties he had referred to in his speech. I said:
Can the minister say whether the Canadian Labour Congress accepts the format the minister sets out?
The minister replied:
We are not sure at this stage whether the type of forum we arc suggesting-an alliance of various interests on an equal footing to discuss national problems- would be suitable to the business community or to labour.
That was the position of the minister on November 24. On November 29, 1976, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) was asked similar questions. He said in respect of a meeting with representatives of the business community:
. . . but they were positive about participation in a multipartite group which would make it possible to have discussions and perhaps agreement on some of the major economic questions .. .
On December 3 last another question was asked of the Minister of Labour as reported at page 1642 of Hansard. I asked:
.. . will the minister now please tell the House what other parties the government will be talking to, to whom he referred in his answers a few days ago-
And to whom he referred in his speech-
-and whether he has told labour what other parties he has in mind.
He was unable to set out what other parties he was referring to, and he said:
We do not know whether there is going to be some real participation by. for instance, labour.
That was on December 3. Later questions were raised again in the House on February 9 this year. These questions were directed by me to the Minister of Finance. He said in reply:
... we have active negotiations under way for a multipartite meeting with business, labour and provincial representatives.
Then he said:
We are in the process of discussions with the various groups, and we have recommended to them that they should be prepared to meet at such a generalized meeting.
Following that, on February 19 the Minister of Labour made his incredible statement about the Liberal Party and its forging a new accommodating relationship with labour, which was of course immediately denied by Mr. Morris of CLC and Mr. Pilkey of the Ontario Federation of Labour. Mr. Morris said:
. . . they now know they were sold down the river by the Liberal government . . .
Mr. Pilkey said:
There is no way labour can find any accommodation in the Liberal party.
More recently, on February 22, the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) repudiated the statements of the Minister of Labour in the House and disavowed any connection with them.
The first question is as follows: has management agreed to the multipartite forum or, if not, to a tripartite forum, or either of them?

March 7, 1977
Adjournment Debate
The second question is: in the discussions with the provinces, has any agreement been met with respect to the proposal of the Minister of Labour?
The third question is: has CLC agreed to the multipartite national forum and, if not, does the government expect agreement or is it prepared to settle for a tripartite consultative organization representing government, labour, and management?
Finally, has there been any discussions with other groups, as the Minister of Labour said there would be as long ago as November 24, 1976?

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-STATEMENT OF MINISTER ON GOVERNMENT'S ACCOMMODATION OF LABOUR-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
It seems important to me not to confuse at the outset two classes of issues. There is, on the one part, the need to maintain a healthy and vigorous dialogue between the different economic partners; on the other part, that dialogue can and does take various forms that are not necessarily incompatible with one another. So the remark by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) that we should come to new arrangements with the Canadian Labour Congress meets the first concern by reasserting the openness as well as the attachment of this government to continued discussions among partners who are not without knowledge that it is in the
interest of all to cooperate as closely in the solution of our problems.
As to the more particular issue of specific ways of initiating and continuing the dialogue it can be approached in terms of past efforts and an attempt to outline a few perspectives. I can say that to date we have had preliminary discussions with union and business representatives. It is still too early to determine the eventual direction of those discussions and what forms, whether institutionalized or not, they will take in the future. The idea of putting the Canada Labour Relations Board or still the Economic Council of Canada back in motion as a meeting point or a general framework for discussions are all so many available possibilities but on which it would be premature to surmise at this point. As to the Labour Congress we know that its preference goes to a tripartite structure but the government already expressed reservations about that.
All this to indicate in the final analysis that we are still looking for-and in this respect the dialogue with the parties concerned is still going on-an appropriate framework for the discussion of government policies. But whatever the final forum on which the parties will agree this government has no intention whatsoever of abandoning the efforts made so far and which look promising.
